tribes: [304a] Peter Freeman, Indian of Narraganset, having been a guide to the English army for the Colonies, under the command of the late Generall Winslow having done good service to the country, and whilst his doing that service, his daughter was taken & made a slave; the Court judgeth it meet to order the Treasurer of the Country to give him two English coats, two pair of stockings, and two pair of shoes, one for himself and one for his wife, a white shirt, four shillings in money to carry him home, having spent much time both now and formerly to obtain his recompense. name_first: [474] Upon the same day that the order past to remove those native Indians to Deer Island, the Wamesit Indians before mentioned being in prison at Charlestown, thirty-three men were sent for before the General Court at Boston, and charged with burning a stack of hay at Chelmsford, belonging to James Richardson. The Indians were first examined singly and apart, and then more of them together, but they all vehemently denied the fact or privity with any that did it; but, notwithstanding, they were sorely taunted at with bitter words by some that accused them; but no proof appeared, and it was afterward discovered that they were all innocent, and that the enemy did it as I have before related; the issue of this examination and charge was, that three of the company, viz. one named Will Hawkins, a Narragansett Indian, that used constantly to work about Salem, and was now, since the war, retired to Wamesit, and two others that were not praying Indians, nor properly belonging to Wamesit, but retired thither since the war; these three were condemned to be sold for slaves, and sent out of the country, and accordingly committed to prison in order to their disposal out of the country; and afterward were sent away. But all the rest, being thirty, were ordered to return back to Charlestown to continue under restraint still.

name_first: RUN away on Monday the 27th of last Month, August, from Gilbert Smith, of Upper Freehold, in Monmouth County, East New-Jersey, a Slave, named Jacob, but has several Times changed his Name, calling himself James Start, and James Pratt, &c. his Mother was a Negro and his Father an Indian, but he passes himself for an Indian, and is like one, of a yellowish Tawney Colour; is about 23 Years of Age, 5 feet 4 or 5 Inches high; his Hair cut short on his Crown, but curls around his Neck; has a remarkable Scar on one of his Cheek Bones, occasioned by a Scald or Burn, and speaks good English: He is much addicted to Smoaking and Drinking. He went from his Work at the Plough and was without shoe or stocking, and had no other Clothes but an Oznabrig Shirt and Trowsers, an old ragged brown Waistcoat, and an old Hat. He came to New-York on Wednesday Morning last, with one Aaron Buck, in a sloop from Barnegat, or Tom's River and has since been seen in Town. Any Person that will bring the said Run-away to Mr. John Talman in New York, Butcher, or Mr. Francis Field, on Golden-Hill, or commit him to any public Goal, giving Notice to one of the said Persons, will receive from either of them, Forty Shillings Reward, and all reasonable charges.

name_first: $200 REWARD. RAN AWAY from the subscriber on the 27th August, at 7 o'clock in the evening, ARCHIBALD HARRIS, a bright mulatto, with coal black hair, resembling that of an Indian, but rather inclined to curl, and rather bushy behind--he has some small scars or knots on his breast, resembling the marks of a cowhide; is about 25 years of age, has a good countenance, but when promptly interrogated has a hesitancy in his speech, and when concious of guilt, rather a stare; has a strong voice, and in conversation talks loud. Was purchased on Lloyd Rodgers, Esq. near the city of Baltimore, in whose service he has been for a considerable time as a coachman, and was raised by Mr. Gittings, of Long-green, Baltimore county; has a forged Pass, and it is supposed he has taken a BLACK MARE, with Saddle and Bridle, about 14 or 15 hands high, hind feet white to the fetlock joints; has a scar on her back occasioned by the saddle. The Mare belongs to a Mr. Knight, on the Falls Turnpike road, four miles from Baltimore. She was hitched near the Lexington market, where he got her, as he was seen within a few rods of her with a small bundle, a few minutes previous to her being missed. Archibald selected me to purchase him of his own accord; he has been my Captain for several months, and had no cause for eloping excepting too good treatment. aug 31 d AUSTIN WOOLFOLK

age: [3] It is well known that Barker lost a sum of money, in amount about $2,000, some months ago. He had buried the money in his garden, and when he went to look for it, it was gone. An Indian servant girl whom he suspected was examined, and though every expedient was exhausted, nothing was elicited respecting the stolen treasure. Barker, it is said, incurred the displeasure of some of the residents on account of the severe treatment of the Indian, in his endeavors to extort from her a confession. The money was not recovered, and Barker seems to have taken the loss to heart and brooded over it a good deal. Finally he arrived at the settled conviction that McGarvey had stolen his money, and accused him of it. On what grounds his suspicion were predicated it is impossible to say, but he had made the remark that he would fix the guilt upon him. It is also said that he had threatened the life of McGarvey if he should find out that he was the thief. This, however, is not authenticated. About half past 8 o’clock on the morning of the 7th, McGarvey was coming down the street near Barker’s residence; Barker was also walking in the same direction, about a dozen paces ahead, when the latter turned suddenly and asked McGarvey why he was following him; the latter answered that he was not following him throwing open his coat to show that he was unarmed, and exclaiming that he was “not a fighting man.”

name_first: RUN away from the Subscriber, in Cumberland, about the 10th of October last, a Mulatto Man named JIM, who is a Slave, but pretends to have a Right to his Freedom. His Father was an Indian, of the Name of Cheshire, and very likely will call himself JAMES CHESHIRE, or CHINK. He is a short well set Fellow, about twenty seven Years of Age, with long black Hair resembling an Indian's; and had on, or took with him, a Virginia Cloth Jacket without Sleeves, lined with Osnabrugs, the Outside striped in the Warp with Copperas died Cotton, and shot in with Cotton and Yarn; his other Clothing was such as Negroes commonly wear. When he went away I expected he was gone to the General Court to seek for his Freedom, and has been seen at Rocky Ridge, on his Way, as he said, to Williamsburg . Whoever brings him to me shall have FORTY SHILLINGS Reward if he is taken in the Colony, and FIVE POUNDS if out thereof, besides what the Law allows.

He is a short well set Fellow, about twenty seven Years of Age, with long black Hair resembling an Indian's; and had on, or took with him, a Virginia Cloth Jacket without Sleeves, lined with Osnabrugs, the Outside striped in the Warp with Copperas died Cotton, and shot in with Cotton and Yarn; his other Clothing was such as Negroes commonly wear. When he went away I expected he was gone to the General Court to seek for his Freedom, and has been seen at Rocky Ridge, on his Way, as he said, to Williamsburg . Whoever brings him to me shall have FORTY SHILLINGS Reward if he is taken in the Colony, and FIVE POUNDS if out thereof, besides what the Law allows.

name_first: Ran-away from her Master, John Jenkins of Boston Mariner, the 8th of this Instant August, a Carolina Indian Maid-Servant, Named Moll, Aged about 20 years, Speaks good English, a short thick fat Wench, having short Hair, is Lame in one of her Hips & goes Wadeling; she has carried away considerable Money, & a bundle of Cloaths, viz. A Pladd Stuff Jacket, broad Check’d a Peticoat small check’d; an old dark Home-spun Jacket, a dark colour’d Kersey Peticoat, & a strip’d Home-spun Pericoat Cotton & Wool; several Cotton & Linnen Shifts, with some others; several pair of Stockings, & several Lace Caps; blue Gloves, and Shooes about half wore out. Whoever shall take up the said Run-away, & her safely convey to her abovesaid Master, or give any true Intelligence of her, so as her Master may have her again who Lives at the North End of the Town in Shipstreet, shall be sufficiently rewarded besides all necessary Charges Paid.

name_first: [25]While I was laboring by what means I might best continue life in my languishing hopes, there comes one Captain Henry Harley unto me, bringing with him a native of the island of Capawick [Martha’s Vineyard,] a place seated to the southward of Cape Cod, whose name was Epenowe, a person of a goodly stature, strong and well proportioned. This man was taken upon the main with some twenty-nine others by a ship of London, that endeavored to sell them for slaves in Spain; but being understood that they were Americans, and found to be unapt for their uses, they would not meddle with them, this being one of them they refused. Wherein they expressed more worth than those that brought them to the market, who could not but know that our nation was at that time in travail for settling of Christian colonies upon that continent, it being an act much tending to our prejudice, when we came into that part of the countries, as it shall further appear. How Captain Harley came to be possessed of this savage, I know not; but I understood by others how he had been showed in London for a wonder… [26] After he had spoken with me, and that I had seen his savage, though I had some reason to believe the gentleman in what he told me, yet I thought it not amiss to take some time before I undertook a business (as I thought) so improbable in some particulars. But yet I doubted not, my resolution being such (as is said) I might make some use of his service; and therefore wished him to leave him with me, giving him my word that when I saw my time to send again to those parts, he should have notice of it, and I woud be gald to accept of his service, and that with as great kindness as he freely offered it; in the mean time, he might be pleased to take his own course,

name_first: [225-227] Upon the Petition of Jonathan Hall Junr. Elam Cook and Abigail his Wife Samuel Talmadge and Phebe his Wife all of Cheshire and David Hall of Essex in the State of Vermont Children and Heirs to Joseph Hall late of said Cheshire Deceasd said Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is evident from the aforesaid Statement of Facts, that if all the various Claims of these Negroes and the several Purchasers and sundry other Persons, And the uncertainty which attends the Proof relative to the true Origin of Descent of said Rhoda, as there is no Person to be found who can from their own knoledge inform who was the Mother of said Rhoda, it is altogether probably there will be contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to have been Free born that she and her Children should be Liberated and set free, and to adjust and settle all the Claims which the several Purchasers have in Justice & equity upon each other and to decree Payment; but if said Rhoda shall be found not to have been free born to Quiet the several Purchasers as per Petition on file &c

Not less than 3,000 people have visited Lent’s room, in Hayward’s block, to-day to see the treasures. It is reported that the company has sold nearly all its stock at $40 per share already. Many adventurers are preparing to start for the new Golconda. It has transpired that an officer in the American legion which left here in the Summer of 1865, under Colonel Geo. M. Green, to join Juarez at El Paso, while on the way overland through Arizona gathered a small sack full of such stones, which was lost in the battle of Zacatecas, when Miramon defeated the Republicans but was in turn routed by Escobedo. name_first: FIFTY DOLLARS REWARD- Ran away from my plantation, parish of Assumption, on or about the 29th of January last, a griff negro man named HENRY, aged about 28 years: is about 5 feet 4 or 5 inches high; has scars caused by cupping on the back of the neck; slender built, resembling somewhat an Indian; teeth projecting a little; has bushy hair; answers very quickly when spoken to, and is by trade a cooper. He was purchased of Mr. Francis P. Winslow, of Mobile. The above reward will be paid for his delivery at any jail within this State. Mrs. ESTHER BLANCHARD. Assumption Post Office, La.

name_first: [624-625]  Shortly after my letter of the 20th January, I assembled the Indians, to whom I had given the War Hatchet, and proposed that they should go immediately upon service.  Accordingly near 200 of them proceeded against the Delawares near the Susquehana, and on the 26. of February discovered a large party of them to the amount of 41. who were destined against our settlements, whom they immediately surprised and made prisoners, and amongst them a remarkable Indian Called Captn Bull. who was their Leader, in which capacity he had done considerable damage during the War.  Him, with 13 others I sent prisoners to New York, and distributed the rest amongst the Friend Indians for the replacing of their deceased connections according to the ancient Custom, the observance of which has added  vigour to their proceedings. - Immediately after this fortunate blow, a small party I had sent out, fell in with a party their equals in number, killed their Chief and took three prisoners, who, with the scalp were brought here yesterday; and this being the first blood shed by them in our quarrel, will effectually widen the breach between the Indians and promote his Majty’s service. On recepit of the news of the first success, I immediately dispatched my Son with another Body of Indians, and a few approved White Men, to take advantage of the consternation, into which the Enemy were thrown by the offensive operations of our friends, and shortly afterwards as I expected, I was visited by Deputys from all the Senecas, accompanied by the Five Nations. These Deputys were charged in the name of their whole Nation to desire peace, and to represent that their Nation, had been led into the war by the artifices of the rest, which they had now discovered, and therefore earnestly requested, that they might be once more admitted into our Friendship, upon which, (with the General's approbation) I proposed to them the several articles, whereof the enclosed is a copy, to which they inanimously assented and subscribed the same accordingly on the 3rd of April, with many promises of engaging heartily agst all our Enemies; for the performance of all which, they have left me Three of their chiefs as Hostages, the rest returning to carry the News to their Nation and collect all the prisoners ettc. which by the articles they are bound to deliver up at Niagara, whither I am by appointment of the General to go in June to make peace with them, and the western Nations, at which time I shal not ommot using all my endeavours for obtaining such concessions and tying them down in such a manner, as will be most conducive to the public security hereafter, and I flatter myself, that the Terms now submitted to by the Senecas will appear to your Lordps to be as full as could well be expected from the present posture of affairs, & the known independence of that Nation.

name_first: [225-227] Upon the Petition of Jonathan Hall Junr. Elam Cook and Abigail his Wife Samuel Talmadge and Phebe his Wife all of Cheshire and David Hall of Essex in the State of Vermont Children and Heirs to Joseph Hall late of said Cheshire Deceasd said Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is evident from the aforesaid Statement of Facts, that if all the various Claims of these Negroes and the several Purchasers and sundry other Persons, And the uncertainty which attends the Proof relative to the true Origin of Descent of said Rhoda, as there is no Person to be found who can from their own knoledge inform who was the Mother of said Rhoda, it is altogether probably there will be contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to have been Free born that she and her Children should be Liberated and set free, and to adjust and settle all the Claims which the several Purchasers have in Justice & equity upon each other and to decree Payment; but if said Rhoda shall be found not to have been free born to Quiet the several Purchasers as per Petition on file &c

name_first: [31] The assassination of Mr. John Rains, of this county, which occurred about the middle of last November, is still shrouded in mystery. The Indian servant who purloined Mr. Rains’ pistols, the day previous to the murder, is still in jail. He has been repeatedly taken out and severely whipped, in order to make him confess what he had done with the pistols; yet nothing has been elicited to criminate any other person. Mr. Rains was bondsman, to a large amount, on the bond of Eli Smith, the late Sheriff of this county, who was required, after the death of Mr. Rains, to give a new bond; but failing to get the proper sureties, the Board of Supervisors appointed Mr. J. A. Moore to fill the vacancy, until the next annual election. Since Mr. Moore has taken charge of the office, it has been ascertained that Smith is a defaulter to a large amount.

name_first: $100 REWARD. RAN AWAY from the subscriber living in Fairfax County, near the Court House, on Sunday morning, the 22d inst. two bright mulatto negroes, SAM and LETITIA, (his wife,) taking wiht them, their infant boy, about seven months old. Sam is about 32 or 33 years old, five feet seven or eight inches high, has a down look, speaks quick, and has some impediment in his speech at times, particularly when confused. He had on when he eloped, a new fur hat, with crape round it, blue broadcloth coat, grey pantaloons; he was very genteelly dressed, and took with him a variety of other clothing. He was my carriage driver; a coarse shoemaker, and prides himself particularly on being a great hand with horses. He can write, and I expect will attempt to forge a pass or some free papers.-- He is exceedingly sly, artful and cunning, and no doubt will make to the north. Letitia is 5 feet 7 or 8 inches high, very straight made, and long straight black hair: about 26 or 27 years old. She has a large white scar on the back of her neck;  she so strongly resembles an Indian, that she might readily pass for one. The child so much resembles its father and mother, that it needs no description. I will give the above reward for securing said negroes in jail, so that I get them again, or fifty dollars for either the man or woman, and all reasonable charges paid, if brought home. GEO. CHICHESTER, Near Fairfax Court House, Va. April 25, 1821. P. S. Masters and owners of vessels are particularly forwarned harboring said negroes at their peril. T ap30--4t

He had on when he eloped, a new fur hat, with crape round it, blue broadcloth coat, grey pantaloons; he was very genteelly dressed, and took with him a variety of other clothing. He was my carriage driver; a coarse shoemaker, and prides himself particularly on being a great hand with horses. He can write, and I expect will attempt to forge a pass or some free papers.-- He is exceedingly sly, artful and cunning, and no doubt will make to the north. Letitia is 5 feet 7 or 8 inches high, very straight made, and long straight black hair: about 26 or 27 years old. She has a large white scar on the back of her neck;  she so strongly resembles an Indian, that she might readily pass for one. The child so much resembles its father and mother, that it needs no description. I will give the above reward for securing said negroes in jail, so that I get them again, or fifty dollars for either the man or woman, and all reasonable charges paid, if brought home. GEO. CHICHESTER, Near Fairfax Court House, Va. April 25, 1821. P. S. Masters and owners of vessels are particularly forwarned harboring said negroes at their peril. T ap30--4t

name_first: This Indenture witneseth that we the Town Councell of Warwick in the County of Providence & Colony of Rhod Island and &c. Whereas Capt John Green of Potowomet ind Town having informed us in Councell that he had a Child born in his house by an Indian woman named Mercey who was then a servant to sd. Green and is sence Dead which child was born ye 24th of March 1728/g named Sarah which is like to be Chargable to sd. Town if not bound out & the sd Green being willing to take her as a servant or apprentice untell she be twenty one years of age which was Consented to and ordred at a Councell meeting held ye 19th Day of Decembr 1730 and that ye clerk to sign in behalf of ye sd Councell. There fore Knowye that we ye sd Councell Do by these Send put and bind ye sd Indian Girl named Sarah an apprentice or servant Unto ye sd John Green and with him his heirs Executor [illegible] or assigns after ye manner of a servant or an apprentice to serve from Day of ye Date here of untill she attains to ye full age of Twenty one years During all which time ye sd apprentice or servant her sd master and mistress faith fully shall serve and his Lawfull Commands every where obey she shall Do no Damage to her sd masters Goods nor see it Done by others without Giving notice thereof to her sd master She shall not absent herself from her masters service by Day nor Night without his Leave nor Commit any act whereby her master may have Damage but in all things to behave herself as a faithfull servant ought to Do all During sd time: and the sd John Green for himself & his heir Executors Admes or assigns Doth hereby Covenant & Promise to Instruct her in all manner of houshold work and to find her with suficent meat Drink apparrel washing and Lodging and all other necessaries both in sickness and in health During sd time and at ye Expiration thereof to Give her two Good suits of apparrel for all parts of her body both Linnin and Woolen Sutable for such a servant or apprentice

tribes: [166] At this Court there was a Weanoke Indian prsented by Captaine Willm Epps wch was taken the last springe at Sherley-Hundred & hath since been wth him and the Court hath ordered yt Capt: Epps doe enter into bond of 500 of tobacco to ye Court that the said Indian shall not runne away, the wch bond to begin to take his force uppon the first arrival of Capt: Epps wth him at ye Eastern Shore: Moreover, it is thought fitt, yt Capt Epps upon his return to James-Citty, wch he intends before ye feast of the Nativity of or Lord God that then the said Capt Epps brings the Indian along wth him to ye Governor to be employed uppon any service; And the Court doth give leave & graunt yt Capt Epps at his goeing for England ye next spring, may carry ye said Indian wth him, otherwise to deliver him upp to the Governor.

name_first: [3] It is well known that Barker lost a sum of money, in amount about $2,000, some months ago. He had buried the money in his garden, and when he went to look for it, it was gone. An Indian servant girl whom he suspected was examined, and though every expedient was exhausted, nothing was elicited respecting the stolen treasure. Barker, it is said, incurred the displeasure of some of the residents on account of the severe treatment of the Indian, in his endeavors to extort from her a confession. The money was not recovered, and Barker seems to have taken the loss to heart and brooded over it a good deal. Finally he arrived at the settled conviction that McGarvey had stolen his money, and accused him of it. On what grounds his suspicion were predicated it is impossible to say, but he had made the remark that he would fix the guilt upon him. It is also said that he had threatened the life of McGarvey if he should find out that he was the thief. This, however, is not authenticated. About half past 8 o’clock on the morning of the 7th, McGarvey was coming down the street near Barker’s residence; Barker was also walking in the same direction, about a dozen paces ahead, when the latter turned suddenly and asked McGarvey why he was following him; the latter answered that he was not following him throwing open his coat to show that he was unarmed, and exclaiming that he was “not a fighting man.”

name_first: [4] Ran away from his Master, Barzillai Beckwith, of East-Haddam, in Connecticut, on the 29th of July last, a Mulatto Man Slave, named Syl, alias Sylvanus: He is about 33 Years of Age, middling for Height, is well set, but is something round shouldered, and goes a little stooping; he wears his Hair, which curls handsomely, hath a thin Beard, is white for a Mulatto, and of an Indian Look: He had on and took with him a Coat and Breeches of plain Cloth, of a Claret Colour, a green Ratteen Waistcoat, a striped Linen Shirt, short Trowsers, a little Felt Hat, and a Pair of Pumps. Whoever will take up said Runaway, and secure him in any of his Majesty's Goals, so that his Master may have him again, shall have Four Dollars Reward, and reasonable Charges, paid by me, Barzillai Beckwith. N. B. All Masters of Vessels, or Owners, are hereby forbid carrying away said Slave, on pain of incurring the utmost. Severity of the Law. He has been travelling with a white Man, who may help him away. Providence, August 10, 1773.

name_first: [53] This is an action of trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment, brought by the appellant against the appellee, to recover her freedom. On the trial, the following facts appeared in evidence: Madame Chauvin deposed, that Marguerite, the plaintiff, appellant here, was born in the year 1778; that the name of her mother was Marie Jean, sometimes called Marie Scipion, who belonged to and lived with Joseph Tayon, the deponent's father; that the mother of the appellant was in possession of deponent's father from the time of his marriage until January, 1801, when she was removed sick from the house of Mr. Chouteau (where Tayon then lived) to the deponent's house, where she died in June, 1802, aged about 60 years. That the deponent had heard from her father and mother, that Marie Scipion was bought by deponent's grand mother, and given to her mother; that she had heard from the same, that Marie Scipion was the daughter of an Indian woman captured by the French near Natchez, and brought [**2] to Fort Chartres, where she was sold as a slave; that a negro man named Scipion was supposed to be the father of [*72] of Marie Scipion; that the deponent has heard this from others than her father and mother; that the deponent's father had an Indian woman named Marie Louise, who had two male children, Akin and Julien, who ran away and passed for freemen at the commencement of the Spanish Government; that they went to New Orleans after the publication of an ordinance of O'Reilly, the Spanish Governor of Louisiana, "declaring all the Indian slaves, then in the province of Louisiana, free at the death of their master, and those born after the publication, free at their birth, prohibiting any sales by any persons then in possession of such slaves; that the deponent read the ordinance to her father, and conversed with him on the risk he ran of losing his Indian slaves, and that she remembers he sold one of these slaves, and was compelled to take it back and hush it up, lest he should be fined under the ordinance; that she remembered to have heard her father say, after the publication of the ordinance, that Marie Scipion and her children would be free at his death, in consequence of [**3] that ordinance.

name_first: [3] RAN away from the Subscriber, a bound negro servant, named Robert Anderson, commonly called Bob. He is about 5 feet 8 inches high, strong made, and about 20 years of age, looks a little dull and heavy, but is quite the reverse when he chooses to exert himself; is pretty fond of liquor; when he is intoxicated is very resolute nad quarrelsome. He has been brought up to the tanners trade, can work very well if he is minded; is remarkable smart and handy in doing housework, which he likes much better than the trade. He ran off the 18th of December, 1790; was seen in New-york some time about Christmas last, in company with a yellow Indian looking fellow, named Jack Sharp, who ran off from his master, Anthony Hubard, starch maker, Philadelphia, in company with the negro. The yellow fellow was born on Long Island, and has a mother living there or in New-york. When they were in New-york, they talked of going to Boston, but whether that was meant as a deeeption, am not able to judge, but expects they would not part far from each other; thinks it probable they may be yet on some part of Long Island. Whoever brings the negro back to his master, shall receive Thirty Dollars reward, or Twenty Dollars for securing him in any public jail in the United States. There is also a reward of 20 dollars offered by the owner of the yellow Fellow, on securing him in any goal, the above reward will be paid after a compliance with this advertisement, on application to

Who ever will secure said runaway so that his master can get him, shall be entitled to the above reward, and all reasonable charges paid.

tribes: The Councill having received information by Major Waldern of the coming in of Wanalauset, with the Sachim of Penicook & Several other Indians now at Cocheechee, & that they have brought in Severall English Captives & freely delivered them, as a testimony of their goodwill to the English & their desire to maintain peace & friendship with us; as also that by order of the Comittee there three Indians of the number abovesayd in hold of having an hand in the Killing of two Englishmen & captivating those that they have now brought in. It is ordered that the Comittee for treating with the Indians in those Eastern parts are licensed & Authroized if they see cause to imploy those Indians to come in in the publick Service against the Enemy having some English in their Company & for that and Supply them with competent ammunition & that they may also send out with them any one of the Imprisoned Indians retayning & effectually securing the other two, that they may all three take their turnes to go out if encouragement be found so to doe.

name_first: [1] RUNAWAY from the subscribers on the night of the first inst. an indentured apprentice to the shoe-making bushels (by the selectmen of the town New-Haven) by the name of Horris Granniss, in the seventeenth year of his age, of middling size, dark complexion, dark hair, rather of a sullen countenance, and quite an indian slope in his walk. — Had on and took with him one pair of mixt coloured broadcloth pantaloons, one pair of black velvet do. one mixt coloured broadcloth coattee, one striped swansdown vest. two shirts, one white the other check, one black knapt hat which was new. — Whoever will take up said runaway and return him to the subscribers shall be entitled to fix cents reward, but no charges. — All persons are forbid harboring, trusting, imploying, or carrying off said boy on penalty of the law

name_first: [4] Ran-away from Andrew Davis, of Groton in Connecticut, the 16th Day of March, last, an Indian Man Servant, Named James Wright, a well Set Fellow of a midling Stature, he had on when he went away, a yellowish Coat and Jacket, a new Beaver Hat, a worsted Cap a fine Holland Shirt, a pair of thread Stockings, his Hair cut off. He Stole a white Mare, Bridle and Saddle. Whoever shall take up said Fellow and convey him to the said Andrew Davis at Groton, or secure him so that his said Master may have him again, shall have Ten Pounds Reward, and all necessary Charge paid by me Andrew Davis.

name_first: RUN away from his Master Eleazer Tyng, Esq; at Dunstable, on the 26th May past, a Negro Man Servant call'd Robbin, almost the Complexion of an Indian, short thick square shoulder'd Fellow, a very short Neck, and thick Legs, about 28 Years old, talks good English, can read and write, and plays on the Fiddle; he was born at Dunstable, and it's thought he has been intic'd to inlist into the Service, or go to Philadelphia: Had on when he went away, a strip'd Cotton and Linnen blue and white Jacket, red Breeches with Brass Buttons, blue Yarn Stockings, a fine Shirt, and took another of a meaner Sort, a red Cap, a Beaver Hat with a mourning Weed in it, and sometimes wears a Wig. Whoever will apprehend said Negro and secure him, so that his Master may have him again, or bring him to the Ware-House of Messiers Alford and Tyng, in Boston, shall have a Reward of Ten Pounds old Tenor, and all reasonable Charges.

name_first: [441] “Know all men by these prsnts that I Andrew Clerke of the towne of Harwich in the County of Barnestable in New England for and in Consideration of the sum of nine pounds to me In hand be fore the sealing & deliuery of these prsnts by Thomas Smith of Eastham in the County affore said well and truly paid of which sd sum I the said Andrew Clerke do exhonerat acquit & discharg him the sd Thomas Smith his heirs executors & Adminnistrators for euer. by these prsnts haue freely & absolutly giuen granted bargained & sold and by these prsnts Doth freely and absolutly giue grant bargaine sell & Confirme vn to him the sd Thomas Smith his executors And Adminnstrators & Assigns my indian seruant cald John Mannases for the full terme of two years & a half from the eleuenth day of Aprell in the yeare of our lorde one thowsand six hundred ninety six thence next insuing. during which said term of two years & half I the said Andrew Clarke do avouch & warant the said John Mannases my servant vn to the said Thomas Smith his executors Adminnistrators & assigns against all & Euery person or persons whatsoeuer lafully Claiming by from or vnder me my executors or Administrators or by mine or theire means act title intrest or procverment, be it farthare knowne by these prsnts that the said John Mannases doth now owne & acknowledg him self to be seruant to sd Thomas Smith half a yere longer then the time aboue mentioned which sd halfe yeare he promised before said Smith bought him, if he would by out his time of his mastar Clark for the which said time the said John Manases doth now in gage faithfully to serue & perfore by these presents. In witnes where of the said Andrew Clerk to his part aboue written & the said John Manases to his part is as aboue writen haue seuerally to these presents set to their hands & seals this thirteenth day of June Ano dom one thowsand six hundred ninety six.

name_first: RUN-AWAY from the subscriber about 10 days ago, a lad about 18 or 19 years of age called BEN WHITEHEAD, he is of the Indian breed and almost white, has coarse straight hair of a dark brown colour and black eyes, well grown and stout made, is a carpenter by trade, and he can read and I believe write a little, will no doubt attempt to pass as a freeman. Had on when he went away a light coloured broadcloth coat, his other clothes Virginia cloth. He may be known on examination by a large scar on one of his legs occasioned by a cut with a broad axe. At the same time went off and supposed with the other, a yellow fellow named REUBEN, a shoemaker, about 27 or 8 years old, 5 feet 9 or 10 inches high, large and well made, except his legs which are rather slender and wide apart. Had on a blue great coat, his other clothes not known. Whoever secures these fellows in any jail, shall receive TEN DOLLARS, or FIVE for either, besides what the law allows. S. KELLO.

Personal property—a negro woman, two Indian slaves (a boy and a girl), a silver tankard). Son John sole executor, when he comes of age, until then the wife, Adam Hude and John Kinsey. To the Honourable the Senate and Honble house of Representatives of the Common Wealth of Massachusetts Humbly Sheweth James Athearn of Tisbury in Dukes County
That in the year 1770 he was often Solicited by one Joash Panue an Indian Man of the Gayhead in County to Procure him a Small Dwelling house built After the English Manor with Repeated promises to Serve your Pettr in the Whale Fishery Untill paid but So it hapened that the said Joash made but one Voyage On the Aut. which your Honble will be by the Act herewith Exhibited amounted to Eight pound and the Cost of the building materials & Labour with Some Other Small Nessecary Charges amount to £27 8 which leaves a ballance of £7 n 8 in your petitioner’s favor on the Interest of which will am. to more then the ballance the sd Joash afterwards Died in the West Indies on his return from Brazill and the Vessell on her return home was taken by the British the first year of Making Reprisals So that the whole was Lost. The Deceased Widow was part Negro & exceedingly vicious has Taken but Little Care of the house more than to bash the Shingles and Every way in a Great Maner Destroyed has Lately Married a negro as bad as herself. I have [illegible] payment but am Denied and answered they had Rather have an Indian Wigwam then pay any thing to yr Pettr for the house your Petitioner

name_first: RUN AWAY, from the subscriber, of Cecil County, Maryland, on the 10th of April last, an indented Indian or Molatto servant-man, named John Moycum, about 25 years of age, a tall and well-set fellow, saws with a whip-saw, and plays on the violin: Had on when he went away, a castor hat, and white linnen cap, check shirt, blue drugget jacket, dark brown cloth breeches, with shoes and stockings. name_first: [58] Vpon Receipt of Two Letters from the Hands of ye Honble ye Governour brought to him by flint a Cherikee Indian living on Cussata River & Caesar John Stephen’s Slave we have this day made a Board and have Concluded to send you the Inclosed Coppyes of ye letters wth. our Instructions and directions to make a speedy Inquiry into the truth of ye matter and give Such Orders to ye parties as Consists wth. Justice and the powers given you by the Act as to that part of ye Complaint wch. relates to War you will receive a Letter from the Governr. to wch. we refer you. name_first: RAN AWAY fror the subscriber, living in Buckingham, about the middle of June last, a mulatto man named BEVERLEY. He is about 32 years of age, thin complexion, about 5 feet 6 inches high, speaks very modestly when spoken to, has a bushy head of thick black hair, resembling an Indian's; has a scar in his forehead, occassioned by the kick of a mule. He has a blue tooth or two in his upper jaw, the side not recollected.-- On the 4th July, in the morning, a saddle and bridle and a sorrel mare frorm the pasture, were missing: I suppose he has got them, and is probably making to some other State--He is an arch, cunning fellow, and will no doubt endeavor to pass as a free man--He went off without any provocation, either of whipping, or threat, or angry word. i will give a reward of $10, if taken in the State, or $20, if taken out of it, besides the legal fees, and he be brought to me, or secured in jail, so that I get him again. If he has taken the sorrel mare, perhaps she may be found with him. July 11 [19-w4w] ARCH'D AUSTIN.

Ct., claiming that Rhodes had not fulfilled his part of the indenture. Tom won the case, and Rhodes was required to pay Tom some L47 in damages. In 1753, Tom, then res. of Southampton, N.Y., sued his lawyer, Joseph Robbins of Preston, claiming that Robbins had never handed the money over to him. The attorney produced Tom's receipt, and the ct. found for Robbins. (Ibid., June 1753, File 162)

name_first: [398-399] The other case was that of a bright, rosy-cheeked girl of twelve, who fell to the lot of a monster, who was never called to any account for her inhumanity. When enfeebled by sickness Rosa became an object of hatred, and one cold, stormy night in the midwinter, sick and half clothed, she was driven from the house, and the key turned in the lock. name_first: One Hundred and Fifty Dollars reward Will be paid for the apprehension and delivery to the subscriber of the following named Slaves: TOM, alias BILL MARSHALL, black aged about 28 years, five feet nine inches high, well known about town as one of our draymen. He is fond of dress, drink and gambling. He will be found in one of the negro grog shops. Very impertinent and short when spoken to. He came from Natchez about three years ago, and has been away since May last. ARMSTEAD, an Indian looking fellow, rather delicate, about 30 years old, five feet 8 inches high. He is a good carpenter and joiner, and pretty well known about town. Has lived for sometime in Mobile, where he belonged to Mr. Cook, a builder. he generally wears a moustache and is neat in his dress. He limps a little, from a sore shin bone of long standing. One hundred dollars for Tom and fifty dollars for Armstead. n13-ct J. P. FRERET.

name_first: RAn-away from her Master James Berry of Boston Mariner about Nine a Clock on Sabbath day night, being the 2d Currant, a Young Indian Woman Servant, Named Pegg, about 20 years of Age, speaks broken English, full Visage, and pretty Tall; She hath a Mark or Branch made in the flesh on her right Arm with Powder, or something else black: hath on two Jackets, one Greenish, and two Petticoats, one Red, yellow Stockings, with Shoes on. name_first: [1] Gabriella and her two daughters, Delila and Henrietta, ask the court to enjoin the heirs of Joseph Bell from selling them as slaves . Citing their "history of lineage," they proclaim that Gabriella's grandmother, Jinny, was "an Indian and free" and that her mother, Judy, was "begotten by a white man by whom her grand mother had ten children born at or near Port Royal Caroline Co. Virginia." Jinny resided with one John Roy and, "either by Indenture or some other arrangement," came into the possession of and resided with "a certain Rodham Kenney." After Gabriella was born, she and her mother "were taken by some legal process and sold as the slaves or property of" Kenney and eventually purchased by "a certain Edward Downing," who gave them to his sister, Bell's wife. The Bells then brought them to Tennessee and received the profits of their labor until Joseph died around 1838. The petitioners represent that "there is to be this day an assembling" of Bell's heirs "for the purposes of distributing or selling" them; "the time has at length arrived when complainants are absolutely forced to assert the right which they have to freedom." They reveal that Bell always admitted their ancestors' freedom and that his daughter, Margery, "has repeatedly [2] declared that at her death complainants with their offspring," who now number eight, "should be free." They pray that the court "will decree their absolute freedom and will perpetually enjoin the said defendants from any interference."

name_first: [206-207] Mr Robert Livinstones Tennants being encouraged by such Proceedings to hold their Farms independent of him was advised by his Lawyers to serve the most riotous of them with ejectments and havg the last term obtain judgments against them The Sheriff of the County of Albany was orderd to turn them out of Possession, and put him in, He accordingly on the 25th of last month went with some men he summoned to attend him, to some houses of the ejected and after some opposition effected it, when proceeding to the House of one Hendrick Bruises, another of the Tenants on the same account one John Van Gelden (an Indian of Sheffield who lives on a Farm there of his own, is married to a White Woman and has by her several children and is a subject of the Massachusetts Government) came there on Horseback with one of his sons and Benjamin Franklin on foot all well armed, with a Gun Bayonet, Hatchett, Powder and Ball and forbid the sheriff touching the house of Bruises, presenting their Guns at him and his company, but the sheriff like a good officer not regarding their THreats ordered his possy to surround them which they endeavoured to do, the Rioters advancing to them with the Indian Yell and other hideous noise, Van Geldens sons snapped his Gun loaded with 10 Buck shot & one Bullet its missing Fire, Franklin made motions as if he would fire as did the old Van Gelden, the Possy still closing with them, though unarmed, knocked down young Van Gelden and Franklin taking their Guns from them, the old Indian being at some distance fired his Piece and shot one Adam Rypenberger (a poor Tenant of Mr Livingstons who attended the Sheriff upon his summons) and rode off but being well pursued was taken and with the other two, sent to, and committed to Albany Jail

name_first: (255) Borderlands families have never had it easy, and the second half of the nineteenth century was no exception. In an act of love and power, American and Hispano families reached out to Indian women and children to ease their borderlands burdens. Lieutenant Colonel King S. Woolsey left his central Arizona ranch in 1864 to kill Apaches and claim land; he returned from his campaign with a ten-year-old Yaqui girl as his personal consort. Lucia Martinez bore the Colonel's children and harassment until his death in 1879. The territorial patriarch left his illegitimate children no inheritance, but he had indentured them, ironically making them eligible for $1,000 from his estate. Woolsey's compatriot Jack Swilling had brandished a gun to uphold slavery, claim Western lands, and make "good Indians," but when his Mexican, American, and O'odham friends staged the Camp Grant Massacre in the spring of 1871, he stayed home with his Mexican wife, four American children, and four Apache wards. Swilling indentured one of these Indian minors, but he most likely did so to protect him from his neighbors' anti-Apache sentiments. Josefina and Miguel Gonzales Roca indentured three-year-old Teutilla in 1869. Of elite families in Mexico and Chile, the Rocas had been nursed and cared for by criadas-mestizo servants-and they wanted the same for their children. When they indentured the Apache toddler, they both continued a longtime Hispanic tradition of dependence upon racially inferior domestics and secured a future of white privilege for their new family.

name_last: [1] Gabriella and her two daughters, Delila and Henrietta, ask the court to enjoin the heirs of Joseph Bell from selling them as slaves . Citing their "history of lineage," they proclaim that Gabriella's grandmother, Jinny, was "an Indian and free" and that her mother, Judy, was "begotten by a white man by whom her grand mother had ten children born at or near Port Royal Caroline Co. Virginia." Jinny resided with one John Roy and, "either by Indenture or some other arrangement," came into the possession of and resided with "a certain Rodham Kenney." After Gabriella was born, she and her mother "were taken by some legal process and sold as the slaves or property of" Kenney and eventually purchased by "a certain Edward Downing," who gave them to his sister, Bell's wife. The Bells then brought them to Tennessee and received the profits of their labor until Joseph died around 1838. The petitioners represent that "there is to be this day an assembling" of Bell's heirs "for the purposes of distributing or selling" them; "the time has at length arrived when complainants are absolutely forced to assert the right which they have to freedom." name_first: [225-227] Upon the Petition of Jonathan Hall Junr. Elam Cook and Abigail his Wife Samuel Talmadge and Phebe his Wife all of Cheshire and David Hall of Essex in the State of Vermont Children and Heirs to Joseph Hall late of said Cheshire Deceasd said Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is evident from the aforesaid Statement of Facts, that if all the various Claims of these Negroes and the several Purchasers and sundry other Persons, And the uncertainty which attends the Proof relative to the true Origin of Descent of said Rhoda, as there is no Person to be found who can from their own knoledge inform who was the Mother of said Rhoda, it is altogether probably there will be contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to have been Free born that she and her Children should be Liberated and set free, and to adjust and settle all the Claims which the several Purchasers have in Justice & equity upon each other and to decree Payment; but if said Rhoda shall be found not to have been free born to Quiet the several Purchasers as per Petition on file &c

The Petition of Thomas Smith of the Town of Eastham within sd Province Humbly sheweth that wheras your Petitioner had an Indian servant called John manasses which in the late wars went out into the service with Major Church in an expedition to the East-ward against the Enemie about the year :1696: and served under Capta Jethro an Indian the whole expedition. but by reason of some ill accidents which hapned to-gether with the remoteness of my abode your Petitioner hath never yet received any wages for his sd service neither hath he sd manasses him self nor any other received for him Which moves your Petitioner to Pray that your Exellency and Honours would Please to take it into your candid consideration and make Efectuall provision that your Petitioner may receive his Just due in that respect. and your humble Petitioner as he is in duty bound shall ever pray &c--

age: [4] RAN away from the Subscriber, on the evening following the 28th inst. an Indian Molatto BOY, fourteen years old, stout made, thick lips, and thick tongue, large prominent black eyes, and a down cast look with his eyes, lisps when he speaks, a bushy head of hair;-- he probably will wear, a striped purple color'd nankeen coat and trowsers, (as he had such cloaths with him) and also a coarse light color'd coating sailors jacket and trowsers;-- he usually wore a brass ring on one of his fingers.-- Any person who will secure the said Boy, so that he can be recovered by the Subscriber, shall have Ten Dollars reward, and all reasonable charges paid.-- His destination is probably to the State of Massachusetts, and his object is to go to sea. Stamford, Sept. 29, 1797.

name_first: Ran away from his Master Mr. Thomas Byles of Newport on Rhode-Island, on the ninth of this Instant June, a Spanish Indian Man Servant, named Sassidillah, but 'tis thought he will change his name: He is about 21 Years of Age, about 5 Foot 8 Inches high, and pretty Slim; his Hair pretty long, and somewhat curled. He has an Indian mark of Blue across the Temples on the right Side of his Face. N.B His Cloaths were found lying by the Water Side on the Day he went away, and 'tis thought he has stole some other Cloaths from on board a vessel. Whoever shall apprehend the abovesaid Runaway Servant, and him safely convey to his said Master in Newport, shall have Five Pounds Reward, and all necessary charges paid."

name_last: [25]While I was laboring by what means I might best continue life in my languishing hopes, there comes one Captain Henry Harley unto me, bringing with him a native of the island of Capawick [Martha’s Vineyard,] a place seated to the southward of Cape Cod, whose name was Epenowe, a person of a goodly stature, strong and well proportioned. This man was taken upon the main with some twenty-nine others by a ship of London, that endeavored to sell them for slaves in Spain; but being understood that they were Americans, and found to be unapt for their uses, they would not meddle with them, this being one of them they refused. Wherein they expressed more worth than those that brought them to the market, who could not but know that our nation was at that time in travail for settling of Christian colonies upon that continent, it being an act much tending to our prejudice, when we came into that part of the countries, as it shall further appear. How Captain Harley came to be possessed of this savage, I know not; but I understood by others how he had been showed in London for a wonder… [26] After he had spoken with me, and that I had seen his savage, though I had some reason to believe the gentleman in what he told me, yet I thought it not amiss to take some time before I undertook a business (as I thought) so improbable in some particulars. But yet I doubted not, my resolution being such (as is said) I might make some use of his service; and therefore wished him to leave him with me, giving him my word that when I saw my time to send again to those parts, he should have notice of it, and I woud be gald to accept of his service, and that with as great kindness as he freely offered it; in the mean time, he might be pleased to take his own course,

name_first: $25,00 REWARD! I WILL pay the above reward for the delivery to me in Perry, Ga., of my Boy BOB, who ran away from me on the first of June, inst., or Fifteen Dollars for his lodgment in any safe Jail where I may promptly get him. Bob is what is usually termed a "likely Boy," about 19 or 20 years old--complected light copper-more of the Indian than negro feature--erect carriage, except when spoken to; he has a down cast look, rather spare in outward appearance, but very muscular when stripped; will weigh about 160 or 170 lbs. He was last seen in the neighborhood of Mr. Colson's and Blacksbear's plantation in Pulaski county, and may now be under arrest, and refuses to give his true name and owner. JOHN G. WHITE, Perry, Ga june 28-t6*

On the trial, the following facts appeared in evidence: Madame Chauvin deposed, that Marguerite, the plaintiff, appellant here, was born in the year 1778; that the name of her mother was Marie Jean, sometimes called Marie Scipion, who belonged to and lived with Joseph Tayon, the deponent's father; that the mother of the appellant was in possession of deponent's father from the time of his marriage until January, 1801, when she was removed sick from the house of Mr. Chouteau (where Tayon then lived) to the deponent's house, where she died in June, 1802, aged about 60 years. That the deponent had heard from her father and mother, that Marie Scipion was bought by deponent's grand mother, and given to her mother; that she had heard from the same, that Marie Scipion was the daughter of an Indian woman captured by the French near Natchez, and brought [**2] to Fort Chartres, where she was sold as a slave; that a negro man named Scipion was supposed to be the father of [*72] of Marie Scipion; that the deponent has heard this from others than her father and mother; that the deponent's father had an Indian woman named Marie Louise, who had two male children, Akin and Julien, who ran away and passed for freemen at the commencement of the Spanish Government; that they went to New Orleans after the publication of an ordinance of O'Reilly, the Spanish Governor of Louisiana, "declaring all the Indian slaves, then in the province of Louisiana, free at the death of their master, and those born after the publication, free at their birth, prohibiting any sales by any persons then in possession of such slaves; that the deponent read the ordinance to her father, and conversed with him on the risk he ran of losing his Indian slaves, and that she remembers he sold one of these slaves, and was compelled to take it back and hush it up, lest he should be fined under the ordinance; that she remembered to have heard her father say, after the publication of the ordinance, that Marie Scipion and her children would be free at his death, in consequence of [**3] that ordinance.

name_first: [485] Captain William Whiting commander of an english ship at his arrival in this country was accused for piracy and then committed to the sheriff 's custody at James City where he has remained and now brought to tryal where it evidently appears that the said Whiting did take and rob a ship belonging to his majesty of Spain now in a league with and friendship with his sacred majesty of England it is therefore ordered that the said Whiteing be sent for England prisoner on the first ship that shall go thither out of this country to answer his accusation in the court of Admiralty there and that in the meantime the said sheriff of James City secure the prison of the said Whiteing and that the ship Whiteing came into this country with now riding seized in his majesties name in Elizabeth river there remain until further order and it is further ordered that all the indians the said Whiteing brought in being taken in the said spanish ship being hereby declared free indians and accordingly to have their liberties.

name_first: [477] Mr. George Menisye Esqr this day presented in the court an indian boy of the county of Tappahannak christened and for the time of ten years brought up amongst the english by Captain William Perry deceased and Mr George Menisye: the indian was [478] examined and found to have been well instructed in the principles of religion, taught to read, instructed to writing: and whereas there hath formerly been given by will, a stock of three hundred pounds sterling by Nicholas ffarrar late of London, merchant, deceased, by the indians, whereof 24 pounds sterling was yearly to be paid to any persons that should bring up three of the indian children, the said Mr Menisye for his better supportation in the education of the said indian boy desires certificate from the court of the bringing him up and instructing him in christian religion as is said : the governor and council approving and commending the care that hath been used towards this youth, have condescended to the request of the said Mr Menisye and have thought good to recommend hereby his suit for the allowance of 8 pounds per annum part of the said 24 pounds towards the maintenance of the said youth and to that purpose in testimony of the promises have thought good to cause the seal of the colony to be hereunto affixed. Given at James city the tenth day of June anno domini 1640.

name_first: Ran-away on the 13th Instant, from his Master David Nevins of Canterbury in Connecticut, a Spanish Indian Man Servant, named Cesar, about 18 Years of Age, tall well set Fellow, long Vissage, full fac’d, dark brown Eye with short Hair, speaks good English; had on a check’d Flannel Shirt, bold Leather Breeches, an old Felt Hat, without stockings or Shoes. name_first: [3] RAnaway from the subscriber on the night of the 30th May last, Levi Dorman, an apprentice to the Blacksmith's trade. Said Dorman is about 18 years old, 5 feet 8 inches tall, very round shouldered, has quite an Indian lope in his walk, short black hair, and a tawny complexion, has a great impediment in his speech; had on when he went away, a redish brown coat, and a pair of striped linen trowsers. All persons are forbid harboring or employing said boy, or carrying him away either by sea or land, under the penalty of the law. And any person who will take up said boy and return him to the subscriber, shall receive one cent reward, and no charges paid. Abijah Tuttle.

name_first: Ran-away from Mr. James Bois of Raynham, in the County of Bristol, on the 24th of August, an Indian Man Servant, named Tobias Peas, but now calls himself James Wicked, about 20 Years of Age. He had on when he went away a brown Coat with brass Buttons and large Cuffs turned up above the Elbows, the fore Parts lin'd with Shalloon, the Body with ToeCloth, a striped double breasted Jacket, coarse white Linnen Shirt, Toe Trousers something short, blue worsted Stockings, round to'd single sol'd Shoes, white Linnen Cap, small Beaver Hat with a hole in the Brim about as big as a Musquet Bullet: He is a tall Fellow, with a full Face, goes something stooping, has a down Look, a smiling Countenance. Whoever shall take up said Runaway, and him convey to his said Master, shall have Five Pounds Reward, and all necessary Charges paid. All Masters of Vessels are caution'd against carrying off said Servant, on Penalty of the Law.

name_first: [53] This is an action of trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment, brought by the appellant against the appellee, to recover her freedom. On the trial, the following facts appeared in evidence: Madame Chauvin deposed, that Marguerite, the plaintiff, appellant here, was born in the year 1778; that the name of her mother was Marie Jean, sometimes called Marie Scipion, who belonged to and lived with Joseph Tayon, the deponent's father; that the mother of the appellant was in possession of deponent's father from the time of his marriage until January, 1801, when she was removed sick from the house of Mr. Chouteau (where Tayon then lived) to the deponent's house, where she died in June, 1802, aged about 60 years. That the deponent had heard from her father and mother, that Marie Scipion was bought by deponent's grand mother, and given to her mother; that she had heard from the same, that Marie Scipion was the daughter of an Indian woman captured by the French near Natchez, and brought [**2] to Fort Chartres, where she was sold as a slave; that a negro man named Scipion was supposed to be the father of [*72] of Marie Scipion; that the deponent has heard this from others than her father and mother; that the deponent's father had an Indian woman named Marie Louise, who had two male children, Akin and Julien, who ran away and passed for freemen at the commencement of the Spanish Government; that they went to New Orleans after the publication of an ordinance of O'Reilly, the Spanish Governor of Louisiana, "declaring all the Indian slaves, then in the province of Louisiana, free at the death of their master, and those born after the publication, free at their birth, prohibiting any sales by any persons then in possession of such slaves; that the deponent read the ordinance to her father, and conversed with him on the risk he ran of losing his Indian slaves, and that she remembers he sold one of these slaves, and was compelled to take it back and hush it up, lest he should be fined under the ordinance; that she remembered to have heard her father say, after the publication of the ordinance, that Marie Scipion and her children would be free at his death, in consequence of [**3] that ordinance.

name_first: LOOK OUT FOR THE RUNAWAY. RANAWAY from the plantation of the subscribers, ten miles south of Clinton, Mi. on the 5th of December, MOSES, a mulatto man, aged about thirty, years, stout built; he went off with the following clothing on: a hunting shirt made after the Indian fashion, a pair of coarse leggins, dark grey color, a pair of moccasins made of coarse leather: it is also believed that he wore false hair, so as nearly to resemble an Indian, whose language he can speak, and may attempt to pass for an Indian; he had a red band or garter around his leggins, and a handkerchief around his hat-- he had also a small book in which was written a few lines. Fifty Dollars reward will be given for his apprehension and safe confinement in any jail, so that we can get him again. He has no doubt been aided by some base white man, and we believe it to be the intention of Moses, to aim for getting to a free state; he spoke of going to New York, to some of the negroes. DORSEY & ANDERSON. Clinton, Jan. 4, 1836--6t--prs. fee $5 25. [Clinton Gazette.

name_first: Run away from Caleb Ferris of East-Chester, in the Province of New-York, some Time before last Christmas; a lusty likely Man Slave, named Joe, aged about 25 Years: He is of a yellow Complexion, being mixed Indian and Negroe, much of an Indian Countenance, speaks altogether English, he is well set every Way, about five Feet ten Inches high, understands all Sorts of Plantation Work, and is an excellent Hand to make Stone-Wall; he was born of a Slave, and brough up by Martha Clark, of W. Chester, and since her Death he is often running about, he sometimes pretends to be free, and it is supposed that a vile Fellow has given him a Pass: He is a great Fiddler, and when he went away, he took his Fiddle and a Bundle of Cloaths. Whoever will take up said Servant and secure him, so that his Master may get him again, shall have THREE POUNDS Reward, and all reasonable Charges paid by me, CALEB FERRIS. All Persons are hereby forewarned from harbouring or carrying off said Servant.

name_first: [3] RAN away from the Subscriber, a bound negro servant, named Robert Anderson, commonly called Bob. He is about 5 feet 8 inches high, strong made, and about 20 years of age, looks a little dull and heavy, but is quite the reverse when he chooses to exert himself; is pretty fond of liquor; when he is intoxicated is very resolute nad quarrelsome. He has been brought up to the tanners trade, can work very well if he is minded; is remarkable smart and handy in doing housework, which he likes much better than the trade. He ran off the 18th of December, 1790; was seen in New-york some time about Christmas last, in company with a yellow Indian looking fellow, named Jack Sharp, who ran off from his master, Anthony Hubard, starch maker, Philadelphia, in company with the negro. The yellow fellow was born on Long Island, and has a mother living there or in New-york. When they were in New-york, they talked of going to Boston, but whether that was meant as a deeeption, am not able to judge, but expects they would not part far from each other; thinks it probable they may be yet on some part of Long Island. Whoever brings the negro back to his master, shall receive Thirty Dollars reward, or Twenty Dollars for securing him in any public jail in the United States. There is also a reward of 20 dollars offered by the owner of the yellow Fellow, on securing him in any goal, the above reward will be paid after a compliance with this advertisement, on application to

name_first: [32] In reference vnto an Indian called Joseph Peter, whoe was comitted to prison att Plymouth for stealing a hyde from John Gorum, hee expressing himselfe pensive for his said fact, and promiseing reformation, was released from bodily punishment; but for satisfaction for two debts, the one which hee oweth to Mr Barnabas Laythorpe, which is 5ll 13s 2d, and for the answaring of the other debt, which is 03 16 06, hee is ordered by the Court to be and abide with the said Barnabas Laythorp and John Gorum, or such as they shall order him to be with, as theire servant, for the full terme of two yeers from the date heerof, and not to absent himselfe at any time from theire said service, by night or by day, without a tikett from one of them; and incase hee shall absent himselfe, hee shall pay four dayes worke for one.

occupations: New York, Aug. 11. They write from Philadelphia, that on the 3d Instant one Lee arrived in a Sloop from Barmuda, by whom they have advice, that the Sloop Philadelphia who Sailed from thence for Barbadoes about the beginning of May last, was taken and carried into Martinico; Also that one Foster in a Barmudas Sloop, that Sailed from thence to Curacoa the latter end of May, was taken 2 or 3 days after she left the Capes of Deleware, by the Queen Ann Packet-Boat that was taken by the French, and was sent to Martinico, in their way thither making Barmudas, the Pilot-Boat went off, and knowing the Sloop, was going on Board her; but one of the French men fired at the Boat, and shot the Pilot through the Body; they took an Indian Slave that belong'd to the Pilot, then put one of the Prisoners into the Pilots Boat and left her, the Pilots wound did not prove mortal: A Sloop was immediately fitted after the French, but they could not be found.

name_first: [1] Gabriella and her two daughters, Delila and Henrietta, ask the court to enjoin the heirs of Joseph Bell from selling them as slaves . Citing their "history of lineage," they proclaim that Gabriella's grandmother, Jinny, was "an Indian and free" and that her mother, Judy, was "begotten by a white man by whom her grand mother had ten children born at or near Port Royal Caroline Co. Virginia." Jinny resided with one John Roy and, "either by Indenture or some other arrangement," came into the possession of and resided with "a certain Rodham Kenney." After Gabriella was born, she and her mother "were taken by some legal process and sold as the slaves or property of" Kenney and eventually purchased by "a certain Edward Downing," who gave them to his sister, Bell's wife. The Bells then brought them to Tennessee and received the profits of their labor until Joseph died around 1838. The petitioners represent that "there is to be this day an assembling" of Bell's heirs "for the purposes of distributing or selling" them; "the time has at length arrived when complainants are absolutely forced to assert the right which they have to freedom." They reveal that Bell always admitted their ancestors' freedom and that his daughter, Margery, "has repeatedly [2] declared that at her death complainants with their offspring," who now number eight, "should be free." They pray that the court "will decree their absolute freedom and will perpetually enjoin the said defendants from any interference."

They pray that the court "will decree their absolute freedom and will perpetually enjoin the said defendants from any interference."

name_first: $100 REWARD. RAN AWAY from the subscriber living in Fairfax County, near the Court House, on Sunday morning, the 22d inst. two bright mulatto negroes, SAM and LETITIA, (his wife,) taking wiht them, their infant boy, about seven months old. Sam is about 32 or 33 years old, five feet seven or eight inches high, has a down look, speaks quick, and has some impediment in his speech at times, particularly when confused. He had on when he eloped, a new fur hat, with crape round it, blue broadcloth coat, grey pantaloons; he was very genteelly dressed, and took with him a variety of other clothing. He was my carriage driver; a coarse shoemaker, and prides himself particularly on being a great hand with horses. He can write, and I expect will attempt to forge a pass or some free papers.-- He is exceedingly sly, artful and cunning, and no doubt will make to the north. Letitia is 5 feet 7 or 8 inches high, very straight made, and long straight black hair: about 26 or 27 years old. She has a large white scar on the back of her neck;  she so strongly resembles an Indian, that she might readily pass for one. The child so much resembles its father and mother, that it needs no description. I will give the above reward for securing said negroes in jail, so that I get them again, or fifty dollars for either the man or woman, and all reasonable charges paid, if brought home. GEO. CHICHESTER, Near Fairfax Court House, Va. April 25, 1821. P. S. Masters and owners of vessels are particularly forwarned harboring said negroes at their peril. T ap30--4t
