name_first: RUN AWAY on the 20th of January last, from the Rev. Mr. Robert Smith’s plantation, in St. Thomas's parish, TWO SLAVES, viz-BASTIAN, a well made mustizo , (or rather Indian breed) fellow, near 40 years old, has long black hair, mixt with grey, about 5 feet 10 inches high, a down look, has the marks of sore legs, had on a blue drab cloth coat, jacket and breeches of white plains,—Lucy, his wife, a very black and likely wench, near the same height, wants one or two fore teeth, had on cost and wrapper of white plains, both this country born, and very feasible, may therefore attempt to get off the province as free, and as they to all their cloaths with them, may appear in a different dreth,— All masters of vessels and others, are hereby cautioned from harbouring, entertaining, or carrying off either of the said slaves. FIVE POUNDS reward will be paid for each, and reasonable charges, if delivered in Charles-Town to the warden of the work-house, or at said plantation to the overseer. And TWENTY-FIVE POUNDS reward to any informer of their being harboured by any white person, on conviction of the offender, by

name_last: Captain Biddle, from Hispaniola, informs, that about six Weeks ago two whaling Sloops, one the Abigail, Captain Snow, belonging to Boston; the other the Sally, Captain Beetle, belonging to Rhode-Island, having put in at a Place called the Platform, were seized for anchoring there, and afterwards condemned at Port-au-Prince; and that there were six Mulattoes and Indians on board Captain Beetle, who are to be confined for six Months, and then to be sold as Slaves, unless, Certificates of their Freedom should arrive from Rhode-Island before that Time. - While Captain Biddle lay at Heneaga he was informed by a Wrecker, that his Majesty's Sloop Swan was lost in going from Turks Island to Providence.

age: [3-4] Whereas the Negro slaves following, viz., DUBLIN, PETER, FORTUNE, DICK, TONEY, TOBEY, MINGO, KATEY and her son QUAW, MARY an Indian woman and her three CHILDREN, and PAPAW SARAH, formerly belonging to Mrs. PATRIDGE, and since in the possession of Mr. THOMAS STONE, late of the parish of St. Dorothy, Planter, dec., and now belonging to SAMUEL PAGE, Esq., have absconded themselves for several months, and all or most of them supposed to be entertained by Mr. THOMAS DOWNES, of the said parish of St. Dorothy, Planter, who several times treated with the said Samuel Page, their past faults shall be forgiven them, or if any person other than the said Mr. Downes, shall bring the said Negroes to Mr. Larson, Marshal, at Spanish-Town, he shall receive twenty Shillings per head over and above the mile-money due (the children and Toby the coach-man, to Joshua Bowes, Esq., only expected) [sic] and whoever entertains them, or any of them for the future, will be prosecuted according to the law. S. PAGE.

age: To the Governor & Majistrates with the Deputies of the generall Court now sitting in Boston, the Petition & humble request of George Danson & Elizabeth his wife is that you will be pleased to consider that I & my wife are both Antient, & that Liveing that wee have is by our hard Labour, which if it had not been for the many Losses wee have had wee had, Nott had neede now to have got our Liveing by our hard Labour. But ye Providence of God so ordering of it, wee desire there to rest Contented, And the ocasion of this our Petition is Because of the Authoritie with the Council Sitting upon the twentie nineth of march Last past, upon this information that severall strang Indians which have been in hostilitie against you & your people, whereof some are Liveing amongst you in this Towne, which were bought & purchased by Severall of your Subjects whereof ourselves are two, who hath an Indian woman wch wee purchased with our money wch was purchased of your Treasuror John Hull about a yeare since, & wee ourselves with our diligence & Instructing of her, hath brought her to be in some measure fitt for our service & Imploy, wch causeth us now to request you the Governor & Magistrates with the Deputies of this yor Genrall Court to take unto your favourable & prudent Consideration, that thereby wee may have Libertie from you as you are our Governor to keepe our Indian woman, which wee have purchased with our money as above said, And if it be your good wills & pleasure to inquire of us any reasonable securitie to secure her so that she may be prevented from doeing any hurt amongst us. Therein wee are free to doe what in yor Judgements you shall see meet Concerning that, so wee hope that you our Governor with this the Generall Court now sitting will grant this one Petition & request, yor so doeing will engage us as in dulie wee are bound Ever to pray for yor best good, so wee are yor faithfull & Christian friends

name_first: [3] RAnaway from the subscriber on the night of the 30th May last, Levi Dorman, an apprentice to the Blacksmith's trade. Said Dorman is about 18 years old, 5 feet 8 inches tall, very round shouldered, has quite an Indian lope in his walk, short black hair, and a tawny complexion, has a great impediment in his speech; had on when he went away, a redish brown coat, and a pair of striped linen trowsers. tribes: [6] There was some rumor of the Indians plotting mischief against the English; and, to strengthen this, the governor of Plymouth, a Mr. Bradford, wrote a letter to this effect: that he was informed, (and did believe it,) that the Naragansett sachem, Miantumnomoh, had sent a great present of wampum to the Mohawks, to aid him against the English, and that it was accepted, and aid promised. The like news was brought by Mr. Haynes, one of the magistrates upon Connecticut, and many words were taken up from some Indians among us, which our fears interpreted the same way. The governor and council gave no great credit to these suspicions, yet they thought fit to take order, strengthening the watches in all towns, and causing them to be ordered by the military officers, (being before committed to the constables' charge,) [7] and withal sent Capt. Jenyson with three men and an Indian interpreter to the Naragansett sachems, to know the truth of their intentions, etc. They were very kindly entertained, but they would not speak with him in the presence of his Indian interpreter, because he was a Pequod, and a servant, and their enemy, and might discover their councils. So he made use of another interpreter.

name_first: [25]While I was laboring by what means I might best continue life in my languishing hopes, there comes one Captain Henry Harley unto me, bringing with him a native of the island of Capawick [Martha’s Vineyard,] a place seated to the southward of Cape Cod, whose name was Epenowe, a person of a goodly stature, strong and well proportioned. This man was taken upon the main with some twenty-nine others by a ship of London, that endeavored to sell them for slaves in Spain; but being understood that they were Americans, and found to be unapt for their uses, they would not meddle with them, this being one of them they refused. Wherein they expressed more worth than those that brought them to the market, who could not but know that our nation was at that time in travail for settling of Christian colonies upon that continent, it being an act much tending to our prejudice, when we came into that part of the countries, as it shall further appear. How Captain Harley came to be possessed of this savage, I know not; but I understood by others how he had been showed in London for a wonder… [26] After he had spoken with me, and that I had seen his savage, though I had some reason to believe the gentleman in what he told me, yet I thought it not amiss to take some time before I undertook a business (as I thought) so improbable in some particulars. But yet I doubted not, my resolution being such (as is said) I might make some use of his service; and therefore wished him to leave him with me, giving him my word that when I saw my time to send again to those parts, he should have notice of it, and I woud be gald to accept of his service, and that with as great kindness as he freely offered it; in the mean time, he might be pleased to take his own course,

name_first: Fifty Dollars Reward. RAN away from the Subscriber in Watertown, Mass. on the 20th inst. an indented servant, seventeen years old, about five feet eight inches high, part Negro and part Indian, but nearly black; had on a long blue coat and new black hat, and wore his hair queued--who stole and rode off a likely white horse, with very strait hind legs, and a small dark spot about the size of a copper on his near whirlbone—followed by a yellowish shaggy dog. Whoever will take up said Boy and Horse, and secure them, shall be entitled to the above reward, or Ten Dollars for the Horse only.

name_first: [95] 102. Indictment of two Indians: "an Indian man called Joseph, an apprentice or servant to Jobe Shearman of the town of Portsmouth, who did some time in ye month of August in the year 1719 Brake open the Shop and warehouse of Joseph Dennis of sd town and stole out a Cask of Rum ... about fourteen gallons of Run and converted ye Same to his own use as will appear by his own Confession." Also of an Indian Lad called James, apprentice or servant to Abraham Anthony of Portsmouth. Note from Thomas Cornell, Assistant, to William Coddington, Sheriff, 17 9/mo:1719, "I send you herewith the Body of an Indian Lad James ... with two other Indians about two or three months ago did break open a warehouse or shop belonging to Joseph Dennis and stole and carried away a Considerable Quantity of Rhum ... I do constitute Joseph Cook Jnr a special Constable for the Execution of this precept." name_first: [32] In reference vnto an Indian called Joseph Peter, whoe was comitted to prison att Plymouth for stealing a hyde from John Gorum, hee expressing himselfe pensive for his said fact, and promiseing reformation, was released from bodily punishment; but for satisfaction for two debts, the one which hee oweth to Mr Barnabas Laythorpe, which is 5ll 13s 2d, and for the answaring of the other debt, which is 03 16 06, hee is ordered by the Court to be and abide with the said Barnabas Laythorp and John Gorum, or such as they shall order him to be with, as theire servant, for the full terme of two yeers from the date heerof, and not to absent himselfe at any time from theire said service, by night or by day, without a tikett from one of them; and incase hee shall absent himselfe, hee shall pay four dayes worke for one.

name_last: [81-83] June 14th Four Indians belonging to the Sault St Louis, having noticed in the little Lake St. Francis, fifteen leagues from Montreal, seven large elm canoes and a small bark one, hid in the wood extending to Chateauguay (in which canoes, according to their calculation, from a hundred and twenty to a hundred and thirty of the enemy might have passed on their way to attack the Montreal settlements), came on the same day to notify the fact to Captain de Cavaltrue, the commandant at Sault St Louis, who informed Mr de Beaucours, the Governor, thereof; the latter issued his orders on the fifteenth of the same month, at one o'clock in the morning; he had three guns fired and the drums beat to arms. The people assembled in the Place d'Armes, where a detachment was formed consisting of two hundred men, whereof I had the command; I marched at six o'clock in the morning in pursuit of the enemy, with ten canoes equipped with twenty men each and twenty officers. On arriving at La Chine, I detached Mr de St. Pierre with five officers, fifty militia and one hundred and twenty Indians of the Sault, whom he was ordered to go and get there for the purpose of scouring the woods next day between the Sault and the Cascades, where I had fixed the rendezvous, which was well executed. For fear of being discovered by the enemy, I waited until night to set out from La Chine for the Cascades. Two leagues from La Chine I inquired of a man who was passing on horseback, whether there was any news? He told me he was carrying a letter from Mr Perthuis, parish priest of St. Anne, to Mr de Beaucours, with information that three Frenchwomen belonging to his parish had been captured at three o'clock in the afternoon that I was going to blockade the passage across to the Cascades. I landed at Point Claire fort, and sent an order to all the captains of the concessions, to march to Bout de l'Isle, to seize the enemy's canoes in case they were still there. I diligently continued my route towards the Cascades, and at one o’clock in the morning, about a league off (au large des) the Cascades, saw a canoe and paddled with all speed towards it. When within sound of the voice, I cried out to them Oukanéguen, Who are you? To the third challenge they answered, Seneca. Seneca ho! ‘Tis for you we are looking. The Indians cried Oukanissé, who are you? Reply. Onnontio Sagojen, Onnontio’s children. The Indians answer; we’re dead. I overtook them with much difficulty; they were moving as well as I. As soon as I overtook this canoe, the three women who had been captured the night before, rose up and threw themselves into my canoe crying and laughing all at once. In that canoe were four Senecas, one Oneida and a Dutchman.  This last spoke Indian like themselves; he had his hair arranged, and was dressed like them.  When the nine were embarked I proceeded to the Cascades, where arriving, day began to break, and I recognized the Dutchman who was closely interrogated as well as the Indians and the three women.  Each, individually, said that no other than that canoe, containing six men, visited the Island of Montreal, where they captured the three women; that Thoianoguen, White Head, a Mohawk, had gone with four Dutchman and thirty-two Indians of the Five Nations, near Chateauguay, to make canoes to cross to the Island of Montreal and make a foray there. As I had sent Mr de St Pierre opposite the Cascades, nothing more urgent was left for me than to go to their cache on the South shore of the little Lake St. Francis, where I arrived at three o’clock in the afternoon, and found seven elm canoes capable of carrying, each, fifteen @ twenty men; all their provisions, powder, ball, deer skins, shoes, awls, blankets, wampum-belts, kettles, &c., which I gave to the nine Indians of the Sault St Louis and sixteen Nepissings of the Lake of the Two Mountains who had accompanied me.  I had the canoes cut; had mine also concealed in the woods, and I lay in ambush until two o’clock in the afternoon of the next day, when I received two Frenchman and three Indians sent me by Mr de St Pierre, with word to range along the bank of the river for about half a league, opposite the island, where the enemy were to pass, in case some canoes should escape me; that I was going to pull up (me mettre en panne) at the Cascades at nightfall to wait for them, and if they did not make their appearance in the course of the night, I should conceal myself in the island with my canoes during the day. At two o’clock in the morning I heard and saw Mr de St Pierre firing at four canoes which were landing at the place where he lay in ambush.  I immediately repaired thither with my whole force. Mr de St Pierre had taken nine men prisoners, two of whom were English, one Dutch and six Indians. An Indian who accompanies me in my canoe made another prisoner on arriving there; two others of the enemy’s canoes made off higher up at daylight; the two canoes were found but the men had escaped. Thejanoquen, with three Dutchman and ten Indians in two canoes, separated in the traverse, and had been to Chateauguay to strike a blow, having missed doing so on the Island of Montreal, whence they were coming. Being perceived by the Indians of the Lake of the Two Mountains, they abandoned the canoes on the South shore. As Thejanoguen was about landing at Chateauguay, he saw Mr de St Pierre firing on his people, whereupon he went ashore and abandoned his canoes, which were found, and he struck into the depths of the forest. Of twenty-four men who escaped in all, only eight reached Coriar; the rest died of hunger on the road.  Thejanoguen got there with two Dutchmen who have been a month sick unto death, as we have learned from a number of prisoners from those parts. After all was done, I proposed to the Indians of the Sault St Louis to go all together in pursuit of the enemy; they told me 'twas useless, that they would die on the way, and, moreover, that we had no provisions, which was the truth. The Indians of the Sault have done wonders, having tied their brethren of the Five Nations, who openly threaten them. I arrived to-day at Sault St Louis at eleven o'clock of the forenoon, and handed over all the prisoners to the chiefs who asked them from me, to make them sing after their fashion. At one o'clock in the afternoon I demanded them back; they were brought to me, and I arrived at Montreal with the sixteen prisoners, whom I surrendered to Mr de Beaucours, Governor, who detached me to proceed with them to Quebec and deliver them to the marquis de Beauharnois, which I did. They are in prison, in irons, since three months. We hear no more of the enemy.

Being perceived by the Indians of the Lake of the Two Mountains, they abandoned the canoes on the South shore. As Thejanoguen was about landing at Chateauguay, he saw Mr de St Pierre firing on his people, whereupon he went ashore and abandoned his canoes, which were found, and he struck into the depths of the forest. Of twenty-four men who escaped in all, only eight reached Coriar; the rest died of hunger on the road.  Thejanoguen got there with two Dutchmen who have been a month sick unto death, as we have learned from a number of prisoners from those parts. After all was done, I proposed to the Indians of the Sault St Louis to go all together in pursuit of the enemy; they told me 'twas useless, that they would die on the way, and, moreover, that we had no provisions, which was the truth. The Indians of the Sault have done wonders, having tied their brethren of the Five Nations, who openly threaten them. I arrived to-day at Sault St Louis at eleven o'clock of the forenoon, and handed over all the prisoners to the chiefs who asked them from me, to make them sing after their fashion. At one o'clock in the afternoon I demanded them back; they were brought to me, and I arrived at Montreal with the sixteen prisoners, whom I surrendered to Mr de Beaucours, Governor, who detached me to proceed with them to Quebec and deliver them to the marquis de Beauharnois, which I did. They are in prison, in irons, since three months. We hear no more of the enemy.

name_first: [104] Wheras Capt John Williams did, about three or foure [caret] since, obtaine an execution from authority for fifty six shillings against Gorge Partrich, Indian, sundry goods stollen away from said Williams, and damage don him, and assisting an Indian squa, seruant to said Willliams, from vnder which execution said Partrich made an escape, and since comitted sundry misdemeniors, as swearing, assaulting, threatening to kill the said Captaine Williams, for which being imprisoned, and brought to answar for said misdemenors, and being found convict therof, was by this Court centanced to be whipt, and warned not to come any more att Scittuate as hee would answare the contrary at his pill, and alsoe ordered him to pay the said Capt Williams the said fifty shillins mensioned in the said execution, and twenty shillings more to said Captain Williams for his charge, trouble, and damage respecting the said misdemenors, and twenty shillings to the Scittuate constabls for theire charges, and eleuen shillings to the vnder marshall for his fees, amounting all to five pounds and seauan shillings in siluer mony; and wheras for the payment wherof Mr William Clarke oblidged himselfe, and on request of said Gorde Partrich hath payed the said monyes, hee, the said Partrich, Indian, did promise well and faithfully to serue the said William Clarke from the date heerof untill the latter end of October next come twelue month, this Court doth therfore impower the said William Clarke to retaine the said Indian, Gorge, Partrich, as his seruant during the said tearme aforsaid, whoe is to find his said seruant with meat, drink, and apparrell, sutable for him, and doe heerby order and require the Indian, Gorge, to doe his master, Mr William Clarke, and his assignes, true and faithfull service, and his lawfull comands euery where to doe, and from his said masters service not to absent himselfe by night nor day without lycence from his said master the whole tearm aforsaid.

name_first: $150 Reward. RAN AWAY from the subscriber in Wilkes county, Georgia, in the month of May last, a man slave, Lige or Elisha, about 22 years of age, 4 feet 6 or 9 inches high, tolerably well made, complected Indian like, straight black hair, teeth (perhaps) affected, somewhat squint or glass eyed. He passed currently as an Indian between Washington, Wilkes county, and Augusta, the last the subscriber heard of him, on his way to Savannah. He knows nothing of the Indian dialect. he may have fallen into the hands of some negro stealing gentry; or more than probable, he may be employed as a boat hand or sailor by some innocent person, or harbored in Augusta or Savannah. The above reward will be paid for the runaway and thief, if stolen, upon conviction; or $40 for the runaway, delivered at any jail in Georgia, or $25 delivered at any jail in the United States, with the grateful thanks of the owner. Johnson Wellborn. March 25. 86 m3t. The Editors of the Augusta Chronicle, Savannah Republican, & Charleston Courier, are requested to insert the above advertisement once a month for three months in their respective papers, and forward their accounts to Col. Johnson Wellborn, Washington, Wilkes county, Gee.

He passed currently as an Indian between Washington, Wilkes county, and Augusta, the last the subscriber heard of him, on his way to Savannah. He knows nothing of the Indian dialect. he may have fallen into the hands of some negro stealing gentry; or more than probable, he may be employed as a boat hand or sailor by some innocent person, or harbored in Augusta or Savannah. The above reward will be paid for the runaway and thief, if stolen, upon conviction; or $40 for the runaway, delivered at any jail in Georgia, or $25 delivered at any jail in the United States, with the grateful thanks of the owner. Johnson Wellborn. March 25. 86 m3t. The Editors of the Augusta Chronicle, Savannah Republican, & Charleston Courier, are requested to insert the above advertisement once a month for three months in their respective papers, and forward their accounts to Col. Johnson Wellborn, Washington, Wilkes county, Gee.

name_first: THIRTY DOLLARS REWARD. BROKE GAOL, on the night of the 4th of August last, a MULATTO MAN, named Thomas Valentine, about 5 feet 10 or 11 inches, a very down, Indian look; had on when he made his escape, an Irish linen shirt, a short brown jacket, striped holland trouisers, London made shoes, silver buckles, and a tolerable good hat; but he may change his cloaths, as he has many. I have heard that he was taken up in Alexandria since he broke gaol, but made his escape.---Whoever will take up said fellow, and secure him in any gaol, or deliver him to the Subscriber, shall receive the above Reward, and reasonable charges, paid by SAMUEL ABELL, Sheriff of Saint Mary's County, Maryland. September 14, 1785.

name_first: RUN AWAY from Roger Saunders, on Saturday the 22nd Inst. an Indian Man, named Peter, which formerly belonged to Mr. Tho: Elliot sen. deceased, he is a good Carpenter and Wheelwright, a short well set Fellow, pretty much mark'd with the small Pox in his Face. Whoever brings him to me at my Plantation at Ashley-River, shall have 5 l. reward, he has eloped from me several Times, and generally has been taken up on the Town Neck. Also run away about two Years since, a Negro Man, named Abram, who is a good Sawyer, middle sized and middle aged, and speaks broken English, he formerly belonged to Major Tobias Fitch, I have a good deal of Reason to think that he is harboured sometimes about Four hole Swamp, sometimes about Mr. Baccots at Goose Creek, and sometimes on the Town Neck, he having been frequently seen about them Places, and not long since on the latter. Whoever apprehends and brings him to my Plantation above mentioned, shall have 20 l. reward.

name_first: [14] Upon an Indictment by the Genrl Solicetor against an Indian by the English Called William a prissoner, for Enteringe into the house of John Odlin of Newport and there in violent manner did bite and wound the servant of the said Odlin. The said Indian beinge brought into Court and demanded of whether Guilty or Not Guilty Ownes Guilty: The Court doe Sentance the said Indian to pay the sum of Eleven pownds to John Odlin for and in Consideration of his loss charge and Expence, and the sum of Twenty Shillings for Court ffees. And that the said Indian be kept in safe custody untill he pay the said sums or other wise give good securety for it, which if he doe not performe within three months then that the said Indian be sold as a slave by the Treasure to Barbadose or Else where by the first oppertunety to make payment of the said sums.

name_first: [2] RAN-away from his Master Mr. Thomas Choat jun. of Ipswich; the 19th Instant, an Indian Man Servant, named Primus, about Thirty Years of Age, middling Stature, well set, full Face, wears his Hair; He had on when he went away, a Homespun double-breasted gray Jacket, his Breeches of the same, bluish yarn Stockings, check'd Drugget Shirt, and Felt Hat almost new, round to'd Shoes. He can Read pretty well Whoever shall take up the abovesaid Runaway Servant and him convey to his said Master at Ipswich have Five Pounds Reward, and all necessary Charges paid. And all Masters of Vessels and others, are hereby caution'd against concealing or carrying off said Servant, on Penalty of the Law in that Case made and provided.

name_first: Ran-away from his Master Stephen Sawyer of Newbury, the 7th of April last, an Indian Man Servant named Peter of middle stature, upwards of 30 Years, he had a small bunch in his Forehead, speaks with small voice. He had on when he Ranaway, a Homespun brownish plain Coat, a homespun sea-green Jacket with pewter Buttons, a speckl'd woolen Shirt, Trowzer Breeches, yarn stockings, and. good shoes. Whoever will take up abovesaid Ranaway and him convey to his said Master, shall have Ten Pounds Reward, and all necessary charges paid them.

name_first: [225-227] Upon the Petition of Jonathan Hall Junr. Elam Cook and Abigail his Wife Samuel Talmadge and Phebe his Wife all of Cheshire and David Hall of Essex in the State of Vermont Children and Heirs to Joseph Hall late of said Cheshire Deceasd said Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is evident from the aforesaid Statement of Facts, that if all the various Claims of these Negroes and the several Purchasers and sundry other Persons, And the uncertainty which attends the Proof relative to the true Origin of Descent of said Rhoda, as there is no Person to be found who can from their own knoledge inform who was the Mother of said Rhoda, it is altogether probably there will be contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to have been Free born that she and her Children should be Liberated and set free, and to adjust and settle all the Claims which the several Purchasers have in Justice & equity upon each other and to decree Payment; but if said Rhoda shall be found not to have been free born to Quiet the several Purchasers as per Petition on file &c

Elam and Samuel in Right of their said Wives Shewing to this Assembly, That on the 6th Day of April 1751, said Joseph then being in full Life purchased of Stephen Judd late of said Waterbury Deceased then in full Life an Indian Molletto Girl named Rhoda as and for a Slave for Life took her Home educated and brought her up and retained her in his Service for many Years during which Time she had a number of Children born in the House of said Joseph who was at great expence in taking Care of nursing and bringing them up during the Time they lived with him, that said Joseph afterwards sold said Rhoda together with Peter one of her Children to Joel Ives, who sold said Rhoda to David Hotchkiss, and said David, to Dick Bristol her husband with whom she now lives, and said Joel Ives sold said Peter to Samuel Clark, who sold him Samuel Bellamy who now holds him, said Joseph also sold Lilly another of the Children of said Rhoda to the Revd John Lewiss, who sold her to John Robbins Junr who now holds her, And said Joseph also sold George one of the other Children of said Rhoda to Daniel Plumb, who sold him to Richard Dowe late of Middletown Deceasd, in the distribution of whose Estate he was set to Samuel Wilcox who sold him to said John Robbins Junr who now holds him, And said Joseph at the Time of his Death left Hampton another of the Children of said Rhoda who came into the Hands of said Jonathan Hall Junr his Sons & Executor who sold him to Simeon Bristol Esqr. who sold him to Robert Martin late of said Cheshire Deceased, and upon his Decease came into the Hands of his Executors Samuel Clark & John Martin, that since the Decease of said Joseph said Hampton Claims to be free, and States that his Mother was born free and was the Daughter of a Spanish Squaw, And thereupon said Hampton brought forward a Suit at Law against said Jonathan for selling him as and for a Slave when he was Born, which Suit went through a Course of Law, and came to a final Tryal to the Jury before the Superior Court which terminated in favour of said Jonathan & against the Freedom of said Hampton, another Suit was afterwards brought by said Hampton for an Assault, against the Executors of said Robert Martin in which the same Question came up, and in a final Tryal to the Jury terminated in favour of the Freedom of Hampton, And the Question relative to the Freedom of said Negroes has had various and contradictory determinations in the Courts of Law, There is also a Suit in Law now pending between said Bristol and said Jonathan relative to the same Question, that it is contradictory Judgments in the Courts of Law Praying this Assembly by themselves or a wise and Judicious Committee to examine into the Facts stated in said Petition and if said Rhoda shall be found to name_first: [275] James Smout of Lawfull age testified and saith that on or about the Twelfth Day of March last part being at the house of Mr. Edward Washbinn in Middleborough being the Same Day that Mr. Peter Caswells Indian Boy did, Samuel Southworthe came in with Richard Durely and They Seemd be very airy & Mr. Washeburns wife Ask’d sd Southworth if he had heard of the Death of his Father Caswells Indian Boy, and he said yes, and farther said there was a cursed Report about it & Mr. Washburn askd what it was She had not heard of it, He said that his Father Caswells going to his Barn and finding his Indian Boy upon the hay-Mow Scar’d him so that he fell down and Struck his head against a Post, and that his Master took him up and truck him against another Mrs. Washburn said she did not believe a word of it, but she beleivd that the Boy died with the Canker.

name_first: [304a] Peter Freeman, Indian of Narraganset, having been a guide to the English army for the Colonies, under the command of the late Generall Winslow having done good service to the country, and whilst his doing that service, his daughter was taken & made a slave; the Court judgeth it meet to order the Treasurer of the Country to give him two English coats, two pair of stockings, and two pair of shoes, one for himself and one for his wife, a white shirt, four shillings in money to carry him home, having spent much time both now and formerly to obtain his recompense. And it is left to the Major General to inform himself where his said daughter is in captivity, and with whom; and to endeavor for her reprisal and freedom, that she may return to her father.

name_first: [2] WHEREAS a Negro Man that went by the Name Toby Hazard, run-away from his Master, from Charles Town, in the Province of Rhode Island, in March 1760, and enlisted in the New-York Provincial Service, in Capt. Wright’s Company, and passed for a free Man; and as the Campaign is now over, he has received his Pay, and absconded, in order, as ‘tis supposed to escape by Sea. He is between an Indian and a Negro,--his Hair not like a Negro’s, but a little longer; about 5 Feet 6 Inches high; and plays on the Violin with his left hand, is 25 Years old. Whoever takes up and secures the said Fellow, and brings him to the subscriber, at Charles-Town, above mentioned, shall receive 20 Dollars, and all reasonable charges paid, by JOHN STANTON.

name_first: [3] RAN-away about two Months ago, from his Master, Moses Gombauld, of the City of New-York, Merchant, one Indian Boy named Pero, about Eighteen Years of Age, speaks French, English and Spanish, but all bad. He had on when we went away, a lap’d double Breasted blue Jacket and Breeches, and has thick bushy Hair. Whoever shall take up the said Indian Boy, and bring him to his abovesaid Master in New York, or to Mr. Stephen Boutineau, Merchant in Boston, or secure him so that his Master may have him again, shall have Three Pounds Reward New York Money, or Nine Pounds our Currency.

name_first: [51] 1735, May 14. Boels, Thomas, of Freehold, yeoman; will of. Bequeaths £40 to overseers of poor of 'Lower Freehold or Topenamus," "the interest to Imploy in the learning of poor children to read, for-ever." Sister, Dorcas Bradford, and her husband, Andrew Bradford. Sister Sarah's eldest sons. Brother-in-law, Robert Ellis, if living. Sister Priscilla's son, Robert Ellis. name_first: [189] Tuesd 19 fair. I was al day at Samll Foxes apprizing & Lt Buttler. at night I Sent an Indian man to prison for breaking into Mr Winthrops house ye night before named Walter Weebucks. he belongs to Norwich. [...] Thursd 21 fair & hot. In ye morning I went into Town & held a Court at ye Prison house. Sentenced Water Weebucks An Indian freeman to pay a fine of ten Shill & Charges 12s. 5s to me & 7s ye keeper & to make Satisfaction in Service. his Crime was breaking into Mr Winthrops house Tuesday night last. Tallman hath bot him for 15 days & to pay in a week – I was at Samll Foxes. I bot Adam for £85. I pd down & gave bond for 80 to be pd ths day 12 month & ye Interest.

name_first: [192-193] Judge Sewall's indorsement does not relate, I think, to a negro belonging to Dr. Cotton Mather, as our Librarian seems to infer from his reference to a statement by Mr. William B. Weeden that "Cotton Mather employed his negro servant." Spaniard was probably the Spanish Indian servant referred to by Mr. Sibley, whom Cotton Mather, in speaking of "the retaliating dispensations of Heaven towards" himself, says he bought and bestowed upon his father, Dr. Increase Mather; adding, "some years after this a knight, whom I had laid under many obligations,"—without doubt meaning Sir William Phips,— "bestowed a Spanish-Indian servant upon me." I have not found in any of Cotton Mather's Diaries the precise passages quoted by Mr. Sibley, but in that for 1681 occurs the following: "Memorandum. About this time I bought a Spanish Indian, and bestowed him for a Servant on my Father. This thing I would not remember in this place, but only because I would observe, whether I do hereafter see some special and signal returns of this action in ye course of my Life. I am secretly persuaded That I shall do so." In a side note he adds: "Now see what I have recorded in the Thirty-fourth year of my Life." This note refers to the following in a later diary: "Memorandum. About Fifteen years ago I bought a Spanish Indian, and bestowed him for a Servant on my Father. About Three years ago Sr William Phips, or governour, bestowed a Spanish Indian for a Servant on myself. My Servant affecting ye Sea, I permitted him to go to Sea; and being an Ingenuous fellow, I gave him an Instrument for his Freedom, if hee serv'd mee till ye end of ye year 1697. Two years ago ye French took him and I lost him : The loss will occasioned me to make a cheerful Resignation unto ye of God. But I was hereupon persuaded, I often expressed my persuasion, that my Servant would be returned unto mee. In the Beginning of the year an English man-of-war, by taking ye vessel, wherein my servant was Retook him. Nevertheless ye captain of the man of war, being a Fellow, that had no principles of Honour or Honesty in him, I could by no means recover my servant out of his hands, who intended to make a perpetual slave of him. So, I gave over my endeavours to Recover him, chiefly troubled for ye condition of ye poor servant."

name_first: [8:165] This Deponoent Testifyd in and saith that Sometime in the year of our Lord 1703 he was Shipt at Boston in New England to Serve as Mate on Board the Ship called the portsmouth Galley James Riley Commander to proceed on a voyage in Quest of a Wreck Supposed to be according to Information Somewhere about the Bahama Island and that they had Shipt on Board to ship ten Indians of Boston aforesd to Serve as Divers in sd Voyage which sd Indians as this - Deponent was Informed now Shipt on Board sd ship by Mr. William Hearley, whom he the Deponent Saw bring the sd Indians on Board. name_first: This Indenture made this thirtieth day of December 1762 between Samuel Ward of Newport in the County of Newport Esqr. On the One Part and Abigail an Indian Woman late of New Shoram in said County Spinster and Jack her Son an Infant on the Other Part Witnesseth that the said Abigail and Jack doth hereby put and bind the said Jack an Apprentice to the said Samuel Ward his Exec & Admin & Him & them to live with and to serve for and dureing the Term of Ten Years next ensueing the Eighteenth Day of January next during all which Time the said Apprentice His said Master shall honestly and faithfully serve his Secrets keep and careful Command Obey, So shall do no Damage to his said Master nor shall see or know it to be done by others without giveing Notice thereof to his Said Master. He shall not waste his Said Master goods nor give or lend them unlawfully. He shall not commit fornication nor contract Matrimony within the Said Term, Nor shall at Cards Dice or any other Game play to his said Masters Damage, He shall not absent himself by Day or by Night from his said Masters Service without his Leave. He shall not haunt Ale houses or taverns; But in all things behave Himself as a Faithful Apprentice & Servant ought to do. toward The Said Samuel Ward Esqr. his Second Admins during the said Term. And the said Samuel Ward Esq. doth hereby covenant so and with the said Abigail and Jack their Exec & Admin that upon the said Jack doing and performing the Several thing beg him to be done and performed. The said Samuel Ward his Exec & Admin shall and will teach the said Jack to write, read, if he be capable to learn, and during said Term find and provide the said Jack with proper & sufficient meat, Drink, physical apparrell, washing and Lodging [unintelligible]  and attendance, and at the Expiration of said term to give the Said Jack a Suit of Apparrell proper to attend the Publick Worship of God in exclusive of his Common and Ordinary Approval. In witness hereof the Parties have hereunto put their Hand and Seals, the Day and year first aforementioned

name_first: RUN away from the Subscribe, on the 3d Day of April, Inst. an indented Indian Man Servant, about 28 Years Old, about Five Feet Three Inchies High, well Made, an Active Quick Fellow ; he had on a Striped Brown and White Kersey Jacket, Long Overalls of the fame, has a Scar on his Right Cheek, made with a Bayonet, is named JAMES TRASHER, sometimes calls himself James Sampson, he Stole and carried away with him, a Blanket and Bed-Tick ; any Person who will take him up, and deliver him to the Subscriber, or commit him to Prison, so that the Owner receive him, shall have Three Pounds Rhode-Island Money Reward.

name_first: I, William JACKSON, have disposed of divers Indians and Negroes unto divers persons in the Summers Islands for and during the term of seven years, provided that in case the Rt. Hon. the Earl of WARWICK or myself shall have any occasion to use any of them at any time within the said term, they shall not be denied so as the time then unexpired of the said service be proportionally supplied by some other servants, with condition also that if any of the said Indians or Negroes shall at any time within the said term unnecessarily absent themselves from their said service, the party so absenting shall for every day’s absence serve a month, and for any month’s absence shall serve a year. Know ye that I, William JACKSON, do by these presents fully and wholly acquit and discharge for ever all and singular the said Indians and Negroes which I have disposed of in the said Islands from all or any other servitude and bondage than is herein expressed except such as shall produce any writing under my hand signifying the contrary and [being] before the day of the date hereof. In testimony &c. 21 Jan 1644. William JACKSON.

She told me he was a Piute. I named him Dan. I judged he was between 3 and 4 years of age. I also bought a Piute Girl of one of the Parvan Indians, whom I judge to be 2 years old. I named her Ruth. I started the Legislature 18th November. Fetched with me my two Indian Children and gave them to my wife Mary, who was very much pleased with the present. name_first: [233] This Indenture made the ninth day of November in the year of our lord 1690 Between trugo an Ingen boy sonn of Quepeg deceased formerly belonging to block island In the Coliny of Roadisland & prouidence plantations on the one part & Joshua Raymond of the same place yeoman on the other part wittneseth that the sayd trugo by & withe the Consent of his Brothers Richard & pettor & his siter hannah hath put & by these presents doth firmly bind himself seruant unto the sayd Joshua Raymond his Heires Executtors Administratters or Assignes for & during the whole terme or time of thirtene full yeares & three monthes to Commenc & begine at the day of the Date hereof & the sayd trugo doth hereby obleige himself his sayd marsters well & truly to Serve from time to time & at all times both by night & by day not absenting himself from his sayd marster house or seruice without his Leave untill the sd thirten yeares & three monthes be fully Eanded but in all things shall bare & behaue himself as becometh a good & faythfull seruant towardes his sayd marster & all his during the aforesd time or terme altho not more herein Expresed In Considerattion wherof the sayd Joshua Raymond doth Couenant promise & Ingaudge for himself his Heires Executtors Administrattores & Assignes to find for and allow unto sayd trugo suffitient meatt drink & apparell washing & Loging suttable for such a seruant during the terme of thirtene yeares & three monthes & to giue him two suits of apparell when his time is Expired & to pay or Cause to be payd to sayd trugo & his brothers & sister aboue named thirtene gallons of Rum & four Crucking Cloth Cottes or fourty shillings mony In manner as followeth viz one gallon of Rum yearly till six gallons be payd to his sayd Brothers or one Cote or ten shillings in the yeares 1691 and 1963 the Rest to be payd to the sayd trugo when his time is outt In witness hereof we haue hereunto sett our hands & seales the day & year aboue written & in the second year of the Reigne of their maiesteys King William & Quene Mary

name_first: [4] RAN away from her Master Thomas Stone of Lovewell's Island, on the first Instant, an Indian Girl named Ruth, born at Ipswich, a short well set Girl has a Scar over her right Eye, and another in her Throat; she went away with a light colour'd great Coat, without Cape or Cuffs, a bluish colour'd close body'd Coat, smoak'd Leather Breeches, yarn Stocking, brass shoe Buckles; and 'tis suppos'd she has the said Cloaths on, having some Time since inlisted in the Expedition, in such a Dress, but was soon discover'd and dismiss'd. Whoever shall take up and return the said Girl to her said Master on the Island, or to Elias Stone of Charlstown, Jun shall have five Pounds Reward, old Tenor, and all necessary Charges paid.

tribes: [447-449] About the latter part of July, 1675, the Council sent Capt. Edward Hutchinson as a commissioner to treat with the Niptuck Indians, and as a guard and assistant to him, Capt. Wheeler and twenty-five of his troops were sent with him, and three of our Christian Indians for guides and interpreters, named Joseph and Sampson, brothers, and sons to old Robin Petuhanit, deceased, a good man who lived at Hasanamoset, together with George Memecho, their kinsman : these three accompanied Captain Wheeler and Captain Hutchinson and were with them at the swamp near Quabage, when the Nipmuck Indians perfidiously set upon our men and slew seven of our men and wounded others ; the Indian, George, was taken prisoner by the enemy, and came home afterward and brought good intelligence. The other two brothers, Joseph and Sampson, acquitted themselves very industriously and faithfully, and, by their care and skilful conduct, guided Captain Hutchinson and Captain Wheeler with their company in safety to Brookfield, an English town near adjacent, which was in a few hours after attacked by those Indians, and most of it burnt. They had only time to get together into one of the best houses, which was the same where the two wounded Captains Hutchinson and Wheeler were, with the remnant of their soldiers and the inhabitants, which, that night and the next day, was besieged and assaulted by the enemy, and divers attempts made to fire it. The particular relation of the matter is declared in the history of the wars, and another printed paper put forth by Capt. Wheeler, being a narrative of the matter, wherein he mentions nothing of those Indians' service, but yet gave them a certificate under his hand in these words.

name_first: [65] Some of the families who claimed Pequot labor in 1637-38 had previously hired Indians as short-term workers and household servants. Someone with the surname Maverick—likely the Reverend Elias Maverick, a relative of the Indian trader Samuel Maverick, but possibly either Samuel himself or his minister father—removed a number of Indian orphans from their villages following a smallpox epidemic among the Pawtucket Indians who followed Sagamore John of Winnisemet. Sometime after 1633, one of these children, named John Sassamon, entered the Richard Callicott household as a servant.

name_first: Run away, on the 20th of September last, from Cohansie Bridge, a very big Negroe man, named Sampson, about 50 years of age, has some Indian blood in him, is hip-shot, and goes very lame; he has taken his son with him, a boy about 12 or 14 years of age, named Sam; he was born of an Indian woman, and looks much like an Indian, except in his hair; both belonging to Silas Parvin of Philadelphia, and are both well clothed, only the boy is barefoot; they have taken with them a gun and ammunition, and two rugs; can both talk Indian very well, and it is likely they have dressed themselves in Indian dress, and gone towards Carolina. Whoever secures said slaves, so that their master may have them again, shall have Five Pounds reward, and all reasonable charges, paid by Silas Parvin.

name_first: [53] This is an action of trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment, brought by the appellant against the appellee, to recover her freedom. On the trial, the following facts appeared in evidence: Madame Chauvin deposed, that Marguerite, the plaintiff, appellant here, was born in the year 1778; that the name of her mother was Marie Jean, sometimes called Marie Scipion, who belonged to and lived with Joseph Tayon, the deponent's father; that the mother of the appellant was in possession of deponent's father from the time of his marriage until January, 1801, when she was removed sick from the house of Mr. Chouteau (where Tayon then lived) to the deponent's house, where she died in June, 1802, aged about 60 years. That the deponent had heard from her father and mother, that Marie Scipion was bought by deponent's grand mother, and given to her mother; that she had heard from the same, that Marie Scipion was the daughter of an Indian woman captured by the French near Natchez, and brought [**2] to Fort Chartres, where she was sold as a slave; that a negro man named Scipion was supposed to be the father of [*72] of Marie Scipion; that the deponent has heard this from others than her father and mother; that the deponent's father had an Indian woman named Marie Louise, who had two male children, Akin and Julien, who ran away and passed for freemen at the commencement of the Spanish Government; that they went to New Orleans after the publication of an ordinance of O'Reilly, the Spanish Governor of Louisiana, "declaring all the Indian slaves, then in the province of Louisiana, free at the death of their master, and those born after the publication, free at their birth, prohibiting any sales by any persons then in possession of such slaves; that the deponent read the ordinance to her father, and conversed with him on the risk he ran of losing his Indian slaves, and that she remembers he sold one of these slaves, and was compelled to take it back and hush it up, lest he should be fined under the ordinance; that she remembered to have heard her father say, after the publication of the ordinance, that Marie Scipion and her children would be free at his death, in consequence of [**3] that ordinance.

name_first: RUN-AWAY from the subscriber about 10 days ago, a lad about 18 or 19 years of age called BEN WHITEHEAD, he is of the Indian breed and almost white, has coarse straight hair of a dark brown colour and black eyes, well grown and stout made, is a carpenter by trade, and he can read and I believe write a little, will no doubt attempt to pass as a freeman. Had on when he went away a light coloured broadcloth coat, his other clothes Virginia cloth. He may be known on examination by a large scar on one of his legs occasioned by a cut with a broad axe. At the same time went off and supposed with the other, a yellow fellow named REUBEN, a shoemaker, about 27 or 8 years old, 5 feet 9 or 10 inches high, large and well made, except his legs which are rather slender and wide apart. Had on a blue great coat, his other clothes not known. Whoever secures these fellows in any jail, shall receive TEN DOLLARS, or FIVE for either, besides what the law allows. S. KELLO.

name_last: [56-57] Complaint, No. 21. Deputy Protector's Office, Berbice, July 20, 1829. INFORMATION having been received that there is a woman named Judith (afflicted with the dropsy) now in the Winkel department, who is entitled to her freedom, because she is by the mother's side descended from the Aborigines of the country, the Deputy Protector proceeded to her dwelling, and received the following statement: Judith, a slave belonging to the Winkel establishment, states,- She is of Indian descent, her grandmother was a Buckeen of the Ackoway tribe, and named Jarverie. She was taken prisoner in a war with other Indians, and sold to the whites; after being so sold, Jarverie has a child, named Quabientge, who Judith states was her mother. This happened in Governor Copierz's time. Judith says, her mother and grandmother belonged to the slaves owned by the Dutch government. Judith says, she now has five children, named Jacob, Paul, Egleton, Leah and Jannetge ; and names as witness to the facts now sated, the free man La Rose, the free woman Santge, and the slaves Roxanna and Gabriel, attached to the Winkels.

name_first: Run-away from the Subscriber, living in Upper Freehold, Monmouth county, near Imlay's-town, on the 22d ult. A Mulattow Slave, half Indian, named Charles Quite; it's likely he will alter his Name: He is about 28 Years of Age, and about 6 Feet 2 Inches high, well-set, something knock-kneed, large Feet, and of a yellow Complexion, with a Scar on one of his Cheeks near his Temple, long Hair, very much curl'd, and thin on the Top of his Head: Had on when he went away, a light-grey home-spun Coat, with streaked Lining, about half-worn, his Jacket is of a more darker colour, and more worn, Tow Shirt and Trowsers, and a Felt Hat: Whoever secures said Slave, so that his Master may have him again, shall have Three Pounds Reward, and reasonable Charges paid, by RICHARD JAMES.

name_first: This Indenture made the fourteenth day of march in the Fourteenth year of his Majestys Reign George the third King of Great Britain A.D. 1774 by and between Thomas Lawton and Marcy his wife and Solomon Ceaser Son of the Saith Marcy all of [None?] Residing in North Kingstown in the County of Kings County Labourers of the one part and Beriah Brown of South Kings Town in the County aforesd. ??? of the Other part Witnesseth, that the Said Solomon Ceaser by and with the Consent of his aforesd. father in law, and Mother hath & doth by these presents put and Placed himself an Apprintace or servant unto the Said Beriah Brown and Amy his wife with them to Serve and will In All Lawful Imployments In Manner of a Servant untill he arises[?] to the Age of Twenty one years old he being Now Sixteen years of age on the fifth day of February Last past all wich Time of time[?] fully to be Compleat and Ended and not to unlawfully Absent himself from his said Master Nor mistress by day or Night, there Goods he shall not waste nor lend, their Secrets he shall Keep, Alehouses nor [?] he Shall not haunt, Nor play at any unlawfull Games whereby his said Master nor mistress shall Come by any damage, Matrimony he Shall not Contract nor fornication Commit within said Time, but the Lawfull Command of his said Master and Mistress [he] Shall Gladly and Every where obey and Shall in All things behave himself as a faithfull Apprentice in all things ought to do during Said Time. And in Consideration whereof the Said Beriah Brown doth Covenant Promise and agree with the Said Solomon Seaser, to find him Sufficient meat drink washing Lodging & apperil during Said Time fiting for Such an Apprintace, and to Bring him up at farming Business, and to Learn & Instruct his said Apprintace to Read well in the bible if he be Capable of Learning & learn him to Write and at the Expiration of sd. terms to discharge him his sd. Apprentice with the aforesd. Clothing and in Confirmation Whereof Partys to these presents have [?] [?] their hands & seals the date aforesd.

name_first: RAN AWAY, from me the Subscriber, of Block-Island, the 23d of this Inst. Sept. A Mustee SLAVE named TIMOTHY, about 18 or 19 years of Age, about 5 Feet 7 Inches high a strait, well built Fellow, of a Yellow Complexion; he had on, when he went away, an old dark-coloured Jacket, and Trowsers; said Fellow went away in a Boat in Company with Two indented Servants, One of them a Mulatto, named CHARLES MOTT, about the same Age as the said Timothy, a stout, well built Fellow, of a dark and surly Countenance, wears his own strait, black Hair, the other an Indian, named SOLOMON CHURCH, much about the same Age as the other Two, but something shorter in Stature, and of a very light Complexion for an Indian; it is uncertain what Clothes these Two last had on; Whoever will apprehend the said Timothy, and return him to me, or secure him in any of his Majesty's Gaols, and give Notice thereof to the Subscriber, shall have FIVE DOLLARS reward, and all-necessary Charges paid; and for the apprehending, returning or securing the other Two, shall have THREE DOLLARS Reward for each, and all reasonable Charges, paid by me ABEL FRANKLIN. Block-Island, Sept. 25, 1771. N.B. All Masters of Vessels and others are hereby cautioned against harbouring, concealing or carrying off said Servants, as they would avoid the Penalty of the Law.

age: [2] INDIAN KILLED.—Near North Fork of Cottonwood, week before last, a most cowardly and barbarous murder was committed. It seems that two white barbarians went to an Indian rancheria in that neighborhood, for the purpose of getting possession of an Indian girl about ten years old. This attempt at forcible possession was resisted by the mother of the child, assisted by a crippled Indian boy, the only one in the rancheria. The resistance of this prior cripple so exasperated the villains that one of them seized him by the top of the head, while with his knife he first cut his throat and then stabbed him to the knife hilt, and to wreak his vengeance fully, turned the knife in the wound several times, then withdrawing it, again stabbed his victim, turning the knife as before, repeating the act until life was extinct. While this butchery was going on the girl and her mother made their escape. In a few days after the fiends burnt the rancheria. There is nothing but the dead body and Indian testimony to prove the above, and though it is convincing, it is not enough, under the law, to punish the miscreants.—White men who live with Indians habitually, should do so subject to Indian testimony; and we think a law to that effect would be wise and proper.

name_first: [4] RAN away from her Master Thomas Stone of Lovewell's Island, on the first Instant, an Indian Girl named Ruth, born at Ipswich, a short well set Girl has a Scar over her right Eye, and another in her Throat; she went away with a light colour'd great Coat, without Cape or Cuffs, a bluish colour'd close body'd Coat, smoak'd Leather Breeches, yarn Stocking, brass shoe Buckles; and 'tis suppos'd she has the said Cloaths on, having some Time since inlisted in the Expedition, in such a Dress, but was soon discover'd and dismiss'd. Whoever shall take up and return the said Girl to her said Master on the Island, or to Elias Stone of Charlstown, Jun shall have five Pounds Reward, old Tenor, and all necessary Charges paid.

enslavement_status: [97] It appeared that a certain white trapper had taken to himself a certain bronze damsel of the wilderness to be his slave-wife, with all the solemn ceremonies of purchase and payment for the same in sundry horses, dogs, and loads of ammunition, as required by the custom in such affairs governing; and that by his business of trapping for beaver, &c., he was, soon after the banns were proclaimed, separated from his beloved one, for the term of three months and upwards, much against his tender inclination and interest, as the following showeth : for during the terms of his said absence, another white man, with intent to injure, &c., spoke certain tender words unto the said trapper's slave-wife, which had the effect to alienate from him the purchased and rightfully possessed affections of his slave-spouse, in favour of her seducer. In this said condition did the beaver-catcher find his bride when he came in from the hunt. He loaded his rifle, and killed the robber of his heart. The grave of the victim is there—a warning to all who would trifle with the vested rights of an American trapper in the love of an Indian beauty.

name_first: RUN away on Monday the 27th of last Month, August, from Gilbert Smith, of Upper Freehold, in Monmouth County, East New-Jersey, a Slave, named Jacob, but has several Times changed his Name, calling himself James Start, and James Pratt, &c. his Mother was a Negro and his Father an Indian, but he passes himself for an Indian, and is like one, of a yellowish Tawney Colour; is about 23 Years of Age, 5 feet 4 or 5 Inches high; his Hair cut short on his Crown, but curls around his Neck; has a remarkable Scar on one of his Cheek Bones, occasioned by a Scald or Burn, and speaks good English: He is much addicted to Smoaking and Drinking. He went from his Work at the Plough and was without shoe or stocking, and had no other Clothes but an Oznabrig Shirt and Trowsers, an old ragged brown Waistcoat, and an old Hat. He came to New-York on Wednesday Morning last, with one Aaron Buck, in a sloop from Barnegat, or Tom's River and has since been seen in Town. Any Person that will bring the said Run-away to Mr. John Talman in New York, Butcher, or Mr. Francis Field, on Golden-Hill, or commit him to any public Goal, giving Notice to one of the said Persons, will receive from either of them, Forty Shillings Reward, and all reasonable charges.

name_first: Twenty Shillings Reward. RAN AWAY, on the 15th inst. an INDIAN Servant Wench named MARGARET, 24 years of age, about five feet high, stout made, much marked with the small pox, black strait short hair tied in a club; had on when she went off, a homespun grey short gown and petticoat, and took with her also, one made of callion. She speaks French well, and English tolerably,-- Whoever will take her up, or give information so that her master may have her again, shall have the above reward, with reasonable charges. GEO. C. ANTHOR, Dyes-street, near Greenwich-street.

name_first: [1] This Indenture witnesseth, that John Simon of Tiverton in y' County of Newport in y' Colony of Rhode Island & Providence Plantations in New England An Indian boy & son to Naomy Zekil of s'd Tiverton hath put himself & by those present, doth voluntarily and of his own free will & accord & with y' consent of his father in law Isaac Zekil of y' town & county a fores'd seafairing man & his mother Naomy Zekil doth put & bind him self Apprentice to Giddeon Gifford of Dartmouth in y' County of Bristol in y' province of Massachusetts Bay in New England house carpenter & to his wife Elizabeth Gifford to acquire part the trade of millery of a house carpenter And with him after y' manner of an apprintice to serve from the Day of y' Date here of for & During the term of fourteen years & five Days next Ensuing to be Compleat & Ended: During all which s'd term y' s'd Apprintice his s'd master & mistress faithfully shall serve their secrets Keep their lawfull commands gladly obey he shall do no Damage to his s'd master or mistress nor see it to be Done of otheres without letting or giving Notice thereof to his s'd master or mistress. He shall not waste his s'd master or mistresses goods nor Lend them unlawfully to any: he shall not commit fornication nor contract matrimony within s'd term: No Cards Dice or any other unlawful Game He shall not play whereby his s'd master or mistress may have Damage with his own goods or y' goods of others He shall not absent himself by day or by Night from his s'd master or mistresses service without their Leave no haunt ale houses taverns or play houses; but in all things behave himself as a faithfull Apprentice ought to do towards his s'd master or mistress & all theirs During y' s'd term, And the s'd Giddeon Gifford & Elizabeth Gifford his wife for them selves & their heirs Doth here by Covenant & promise to teach & instruct or Cause y' s'd apprentice to be taught & Instructed in y' art trade or calling of a house carpenter by the best ways or means he or they can within y' s'd term finding unto ye s'd apprentice good & sufficient meat drink apperel washing & lodging suitable for for such an apprintice both in sickness & in helth During s'd term & also to Teach or Cause y' s'd apprintice to be taught to Read & Wright English with In the s'd term And at y' Expiration to give unto y' s'd apprintice one good New suite of apperel for all parts of his body besides his Daily wareing cloths And as many carpenters tools of such sorts as he shall Chose as shall be worth three pounds old tenner &c. In testimony whereof the parties to these presents have hereunto interchangeably set their hands & seals the twenty second day of June in y' twenty fifth year of his majesties reign George y' second, King of Great Britian France & Ireland &c. Anno Domini 1751.

He shall not waste his s'd master or mistresses goods nor Lend them unlawfully to any: he shall not commit fornication nor contract matrimony within s'd term: No Cards Dice or any other unlawful Game He shall not play whereby his s'd master or mistress may have Damage with his own goods or y' goods of others He shall not absent himself by day or by Night from his s'd master or mistresses service without their Leave no haunt ale houses taverns or play houses; but in all things behave himself as a faithfull Apprentice ought to do towards his s'd master or mistress & all theirs During y' s'd term, And the s'd Giddeon Gifford & Elizabeth Gifford his wife for them selves & their heirs Doth here by Covenant & promise to teach & instruct or Cause y' s'd apprentice to be taught & Instructed in y' art trade or calling of a house carpenter by the best ways or means he or they can within y' s'd term finding unto ye s'd apprentice good & sufficient meat drink apperel washing & lodging suitable for for such an apprintice both in sickness & in helth During s'd term & also to Teach or Cause y' s'd apprintice to be taught to Read & Wright English with In the s'd term And at y' Expiration to give unto y' s'd apprintice one good New suite of apperel for all parts of his body besides his Daily wareing cloths And as many carpenters tools of such sorts as he shall Chose as shall be worth three pounds old tenner &c. In testimony whereof the parties to these presents have hereunto interchangeably set their hands & seals the twenty second day of June in y' twenty fifth year of his majesties reign George y' second, King of Great Britian France & Ireland &c. name_first: [322] Articles of Agreement made and fully concluded upon 21 Sep 1675 between Elizabeth STIRRUP, the one party, and Marie SCADDING, the other party, both of the parish of St. George’s which are as follows: Imprimis: The said Elizabeth STIRRUP doth consent and agree that her Indian woman, Nan by name, shall be married unto Marie SCADDING’s Indian man, Robert by name. And both Elizabeth and Marie are to have what children it shall please God the said Nan and Robert shall have while man and wife: the said Elizabeth shall have the first child, be it male or female, and Marie the next, and so in course as it shall please God they have children. And if it so please God that the said Indian woman should have two children at one birth, then Elizabeth to have one and Marie the other child, be it male of female.

name_first: To the Governor & Majistrates with the Deputies of the generall Court now sitting in Boston, the Petition & humble request of George Danson & Elizabeth his wife is that you will be pleased to consider that I & my wife are both Antient, & that Liveing that wee have is by our hard Labour, which if it had not been for the many Losses wee have had wee had, Nott had neede now to have got our Liveing by our hard Labour. But ye Providence of God so ordering of it, wee desire there to rest Contented, And the ocasion of this our Petition is Because of the Authoritie with the Council Sitting upon the twentie nineth of march Last past, upon this information that severall strang Indians which have been in hostilitie against you & your people, whereof some are Liveing amongst you in this Towne, which were bought & purchased by Severall of your Subjects whereof ourselves are two, who hath an Indian woman wch wee purchased with our money wch was purchased of your Treasuror John Hull about a yeare since, & wee ourselves with our diligence & Instructing of her, hath brought her to be in some measure fitt for our service & Imploy, wch causeth us now to request you the Governor & Magistrates with the Deputies of this yor Genrall Court to take unto your favourable & prudent Consideration, that thereby wee may have Libertie from you as you are our Governor to keepe our Indian woman, which wee have purchased with our money as above said, And if it be your good wills & pleasure to inquire of us any reasonable securitie to secure her so that she may be prevented from doeing any hurt amongst us. Therein wee are free to doe what in yor Judgements you shall see meet Concerning that, so wee hope that you our Governor with this the Generall Court now sitting will grant this one Petition & request, yor so doeing will engage us as in dulie wee are bound Ever to pray for yor best good, so wee are yor faithfull & Christian friends

name_first: [370] 744. Nathan Bull, mariner, and Joseph Scott, merchant, both of Newport, vs. Joseph Power of Newport, mariner, for £200 damages for unlawfully enticing away a molatto man servant named James Dunbar belonging to the plaintiffs. Indenture dated 4 June 1741: James Dunbar a mulatto man now residing in Newport, for £70 paid by Nathan Bull, mariner, and Joseph Scott, merchant, bound himself for 5 years; signed J, witnessed by Walt'r Chapman and James Davis. Deposition of William Tosh of Newport, that he being Capt. Quartermaster on the brig Victory whereof Joseph Power was commander, 'did on the 18th day of May see the molatto fellow named James Dunbar on bord ... heard Capt. Power say he knew sd molatto at Suranam ... knew him to be a servant ... next day when we came to sail sd Dunbar was upon deck and was active in getting under sail ... acted as hand on board ... till arrival at Isle of Blanes [blanco?] and then he ran away from sd brig ... going ashore in boat to get wood for vessell's use.' Deposition of William Allen of Newport, Lieut. of brig Victory, that at the Island Blanco he heard Capt. Power 'desire some people that were at sd Island Turtling to catch sd Fellow for him & the Brig went under sail & stood to sea & in the night we tacked and stood in [371] again for the Island with a Design as the Capt. told me to go to the same Place & see if those Turtlers had not caught sd Fellow ... but we could not fetch the Island again then by strong Leward current.' John Mawdsly of Newport, mariner, deposed that he was at Suranam [sic] in November 1741 and come from thence with Capt. Joseph Power as a mariner to this place ... while at Suranam saw mulatto fellow on board. Other depositions made by Peter Marshall of Newport, mariner, William Edmunds (signed X), Stephen Tripp of Newport, and Samuel Scranton of Newport. Plaintiff awarded £100; verdict appealed.

name_last: ONE HUNDRED DOLLARS REWARD-I will pay One Hundred Dollars for the delivery of my slave MARTHA in the Work House of the First District. She is the wife of a black man named Jim White, who went to California last summer with a Mr. Perry Collins. She is a dark mulattress or light griffon, about 20 years old, rather small shoulders, and slender made, about the middle height, with features somewhat resembling the Indian. She was formerly in the employ of a Mrs. Collins, on Phillipps street, near Live Oak street, Lafayette. I warn all persons against hireing or harboring her, under the penalty of the law.

name_first: [1] This Indenture made this 1st day of September in the fourteenth year of his Majts Reign George the second King of Great Britain Anno Dom. 1740 by and between To: Dotheage & his squaw Dinah an Indian Man & Indian Woman of Westerly in Kings County & Colony of Rhode-Island of the one part and Content Babcock Widow and Relict of Capt. James Babcock Late of sd. Westerly deceased: of the other part Witnesesseth that the sd. To & Dinah doth by these presents of their own free will & Accord and for divers good causes & Considerations moving it hereunto Bind our Son named Jo: an Apprentice or Servant unto the above named Content Babcock to serve her or her Heirs or Assigns for and during the full term of Time until the sd. Apprentice shall arrive to the full age of twenty one Years (he being 14 months old & 20 days now) During all which term of Time as aforesd. the sd. Servant shall faithfully serve his sd. mistress her Heirs or Assigns their Lawful Commands Every where gladly obey he shall not absent himself Day nor Night out of their service with-out Leave he shall not haunt Taverns, Commit Fornication nor contract matrimony within said Term of Time but in all Things behave himself as a Good and Faithful Servant ought to do During sd. Servitude. And the sd. Content Babcock doth by these Presents Promise for herself her Heirs or Assigns to find and Provide for said Apprentice Convenient Meat, Drink, Clothing, Washing & Lodging During said Term & cause him to be Learnt to Read & at the end & Expiration of sd. Term of Time being faithfully performed to Give unto the said Servant two suits of cloaths for all parts of his Body that is to say one New Suit besides his common Cloathing & five Pounds in Money In Witness whereof we have herunto set our Hands & Seals the Day & Year before Written

name_first: Allow me to inform you of a most inhuman outrage that took place here last Wednesday morning. A young man living here in town hired an Indian to go with him after a load of barley. When about one-fourth of a mile on their way, they met one Bob Hildreth, who claimed the Indian as his property and asked the Indian where in h—ll he was going. The Indian answering, after barley, he told him to get out of the wagon d—d quick; that he would show him the way to come home. He made the Indian cross his hands behind, when he fastened them with his rope, swearing he would drag him to death. Then, mounting his horse and taking two half hitches around the logger head of his saddle, he put spurs to his horse, throwing the Indian eight or ten feet, with a hard fall—the Indian screaming and begging for his life. The horse, after going some few jumps, became frightened and threw Hildreth off. The rope being tied would not come loose, the horse running zigzag across the road and crossing two ditches before he was caught. The Indian was terribly mangled, his arms being twisted off in his shoulders. So much for slavery in California. Jarboe, the great Indian hunter of Humboldt, who is now dead, claimed to have had those Indians bound to him by one of the most cursed of all laws that ever were passed in this State. Hildreth, buying the property of Mrs. Jarboe, now claims these Indians as part of the estate. She setting the Indians free to go where they please, they will not stay with Hildreth, nor has he any right to them. The Legislature has done much blowing concerning the Indians in this county, but every Act hits them harder.

name_first: RUN-AWAY from their Masters, (Col. Job Almy, and Cornelius Sole, both of Tiverton) on the 2d Day of November Instant, two Negro Men and one Indian Man, Slaves, all born in Tiverton, described as follows, viz.—Pero, one of the Negroes, about 25 Years of Age, is a Blacksmith by Trade, and plays on a Fiddle; had on when he went away, a Sheeps gray Coat, with blue Cuffs, a striped Flannel Jacket, Leather Breeches, thick Shoes, a Hat, and a full Cap.—Jack, (the other Negro) about 35 Years of Age, 5 Feet 6 Inches high, has a Scar on his Forehead, and has a glaring Eye; had on a mill'd Worsted Coat, white Holland Jacket, a striped Flannel ditto, Fustian Breeches, and a Pair of thin Shoes. —Isaac, (the Indian) about 28 Years old, 5 Feet 10 Inches high, was born of a Spanish Squaw, has a Scar in his Forehead; had on a mill'd colour'd Coat, a short Jacket near the same Colour, a Pair of Tow Trowsers, and a Pair of thin Shoes.

age: [215] Don’t ask me to describe dinners, that is out of my line. The dinner was quite ordinary—two or three courses. The waiters were three Digger Indians, of the homeliest kind, two young squaws, and a boy—far from neat, yet tolerably handy. After dinner Mrs. Hastings bragged of her Indians, told me all their merits and demerits. Admired them as servants, but not as cooks—she has a Chinaman cook. So are the races mixed up here. Judge Hastings is a convert to the Roman church; his wife is a leading Presbyterian here. He, like all proselytes, is very zealous, is probably the most influential man in that church here. He had traveled abroad, and gave us a most interesting description of his presentation to the Pope.

name_first: I, Philip LEA of Bermoda als Sommer Islands do alienate, bargain and sell unto Lazarus OWEN, planter, one Indian child called by the name of ffrances, the produce of my Indian man James and his wife, and Indian belonging to Capt. WILLIAMS and now resident in his house, unto the said Lazarus as his own proper goods and chattels vizt all that right, title, interest, and claim, that I, the said Philip LEA, my heirs &c. shall have thereunto. But in case the child shall die within one year and one day [?], that then the said loss thereof shall be the said Philip LEA’s, and return unto the said Lazarus £8 6s either in money or goods within one year and one day after the decease of the said child. And for the true performance whereof I bind me my heirs, &c. formally by these presents. In witness &c. Signed Philip LEA. 17? Apr 1657. Teste Anthony JENOUR, Secretary.
